bank.q: Your support agent's loop exits when the assistant's text contains the word "resolved", or after a hard cap of 5 iterations. In production it sometimes stops mid-refund because it said "this will be resolved shortly", and sometimes keeps calling tools after the customer's issue is finished. Which loop-control mechanism is MOST appropriate?
o: Raise the iteration cap from 5 to 20 so the agent has more room to finish, keeping the "resolved" check as the main exit
Continue while `stop_reason` is "tool_use" and stop on "end_turn", appending each tool result to the history between iterations
Expand the keyword check to a list of completion phrases such as "resolved", "done" and "all set", matched only at the end of the text
Terminate the loop as soon as any tool call returns successfully, since a successful call means the requested action took place
bank.w: The model signals its own state: "tool_use" means it needs tool results to continue, "end_turn" means it has finished, so the loop neither stops mid-task nor runs past completion; appending each result keeps the next decision informed. Why not the others: A keeps an arbitrary cap and still parses text, so both observed failures remain; C is still parsing natural language, which the phrase "will be resolved shortly" already broke; D stops after the first success even when more steps are pending.

bank.q: Your research coordinator's loop exits after a hard cap of 3 model turns. On broad topics it stops before the report generation subagent runs, and stakeholders receive truncated reports. A teammate's first fix, raising the cap, only moved the truncation to longer topics. Runs must end when the work is complete, without risking runaway loops. Which is the MOST appropriate primary stopping mechanism?
o: Replace the cap of 3 with a fixed cap of 10 turns for every query, tuned from the longest topic observed in last month's logs
Stop once the assistant's text contains the phrase "final report", which the system prompt instructs it to emit when finished
Stop as soon as the synthesis subagent returns any output, since synthesis is the last analytical step before reporting
Continue while `stop_reason` is "tool_use" and exit on "end_turn", keeping a generous turn cap only as a safety backstop
bank.w: Termination should follow the model's own signal: "end_turn" means the work is done, while "tool_use" means it still needs tool results. A generous cap stays useful only as a backstop against runaway loops, which covers the second constraint. Why not the others: A is still an arbitrary cap as the primary control, and the teammate's experience shows it only moves the truncation; B parses natural-language output to decide completion, a documented anti-pattern that fails whenever the phrase is missing or appears early; C stops before the report generation subagent runs, reproducing the very truncation being fixed.

bank.q: Your coordinator sends two search subagents the same broad prompt, "research renewable energy policy", to run in parallel. Their results overlap heavily: about 60% of the sources appear in both, and token spend per report has nearly doubled without broader coverage. The team wants to keep parallel execution. Which change BEST addresses the duplication?
o: Partition the scope before delegating, giving each search subagent a distinct subtopic or source type so their work does not overlap
Let both subagents run as they do now and have the synthesis subagent deduplicate the overlapping sources before writing the report
Reduce the system to a single search subagent and accept slower research, since one agent can never duplicate its own work
Run the two search subagents sequentially, passing the first one's source list to the second so it can skip what is already found
bank.w: Duplication starts at delegation: identical broad prompts invite identical searches. Partitioning the scope by subtopic or source type removes the overlap at its source while keeping both subagents working in parallel, as the team requires. Why not the others: B deduplicates only after the tokens are already spent; C gives up parallelism and the throughput it provides; D also abandons parallel execution and still leaves the second agent guessing at overlap from a list of sources.

bank.q: Your research coordinator receives the synthesis draft for a report on battery recycling. Its evaluation step finds that one of the five required subtopics, regulatory frameworks, has no coverage at all, while the other four are well supported with citations. Search and analysis took 40 minutes, and the report is due today. What orchestration pattern BEST resolves the gap?
o: Ship the report on time with an explicit note telling stakeholders that the regulatory frameworks subtopic is not yet covered
Restart the entire pipeline from the original query with a revised prompt that emphasizes regulatory frameworks more strongly
Re-delegate targeted queries on the missing subtopic to the search and analysis subagents, then re-run synthesis until coverage is complete
Have the report generation subagent write the missing section from its own general knowledge, so no additional search is needed
bank.w: An iterative refinement loop is the designed fix: the coordinator evaluates the synthesis for gaps, sends targeted queries for just the missing subtopic, and re-invokes synthesis. That reuses the 40 minutes of completed work and fits the deadline. Why not the others: A ships a known gap in a required subtopic; B throws away four well-supported subtopics and repeats all the work; D fabricates content without sources, so the new section has no citations to back it.

bank.q: Telemetry shows 70% of queries to your research system are single-fact lookups such as "What year was the framework released?", yet the coordinator sends every query through search, analysis, synthesis and report generation, averaging 60 s and about 5x the tokens of a direct search. Complex topics must keep their full depth. Which design BEST addresses this?
o: Cache full-pipeline results by query text, so that repeated simple lookups return instantly instead of running every stage again
Have the coordinator assess each query's complexity and invoke only the subagents it needs, keeping the full pipeline for complex topics
Keep the full pipeline for every query but cut each subagent's token budget when the query looks short, to lower the per-query cost
Remove the analysis and report generation subagents permanently, since most queries need only a search and a short direct answer
bank.w: A coordinator should select subagents dynamically, matching effort to the query: a simple lookup needs one search subagent, while complex topics still get the whole pipeline, which satisfies the depth constraint. Why not the others: A helps only exact repeats, so first-time simple queries still pay the full 60 s, and it adds invalidation work; C still runs every stage and risks starving complex queries that happen to be short; D breaks the complex topics that must keep their full depth.

bank.q: You run the research system on "the global shift to renewable energy". Every subagent reports success and the final report is coherent, but it covers only solar power, omitting wind, hydro and geothermal. The coordinator's log shows it decomposed the topic into "residential solar", "utility-scale solar" and "solar manufacturing". What is the MOST likely root cause?
o: The coordinator's decomposition was too narrow: all three subtopics are solar, so the other energy sources were never assigned to anyone
The search subagent's queries were not comprehensive enough and need broader keywords that cover more sectors of the energy market
The synthesis subagent dropped the wind, hydro and geothermal findings while aggregating results, keeping only the solar material
The document analysis subagent's relevance criteria were too strict and filtered out non-solar sources before they reached synthesis
bank.w: The log is the decisive cue: every subtopic the coordinator assigned is about solar, so wind, hydro and geothermal were never researched, while the subagents did exactly what they were asked. The fix belongs upstream, in the decomposition. Why not the others: B blames search, which correctly searched the solar subtopics it received; C assumes findings that were never produced, since no subagent researched other sources; D likewise blames a filter for material that was never in scope.

bank.q: Your research coordinator needs results from three independent searches (academic papers, industry reports and news) before synthesis. Today it issues one `Task` call per turn and waits for each result, so the search phase takes about 3 minutes. The searches share no dependencies. How should the coordinator spawn them so they run in parallel?
o: Set `tool_choice` to "any" on the coordinator's request so the model is pushed to issue all three searches at the same time
Call `fork_session` three times from the coordinator's current state, creating one independent branch for each of the searches
Lower each search subagent's timeout so all three return faster, letting the coordinator move through its turns more quickly
Emit three `Task` calls in a single coordinator response, since calls in one response run in parallel rather than one per turn
bank.w: Parallel subagents come from emitting several `Task` calls in one coordinator response; issuing one call per turn, as the coordinator does now, runs them sequentially. With no dependencies between the searches, nothing forces them to wait. Why not the others: A only forces the model to call some tool, not to call several at once; B is for branching a session to explore alternatives from shared context, not for parallel delegation; C may shorten each call but leaves them strictly sequential.

bank.q: Your developer productivity coordinator is meant to delegate code search and test analysis to specialized subagents, but logs show it never delegates and does every task itself, filling its context. A teammate added few-shot delegation examples to its prompt with no effect. A config review shows its `allowedTools` list omits "Task". What is the BEST fix?
o: Add more few-shot examples to the system prompt, each showing the coordinator delegating one kind of task to the matching subagent
Increase the number of subagents in the coordinator's `AgentDefinition` so there are more specialists available to receive the work
Add "Task" to the coordinator's `allowedTools`, since the `Task` tool is how subagents are spawned and must be permitted to delegate
Rewrite the coordinator prompt with step-by-step procedural instructions that spell out when and how each subagent must be called
bank.w: The `Task` tool is the mechanism that spawns subagents, so a coordinator whose `allowedTools` omits it cannot delegate however it is prompted; the teammate's failed few-shot attempt confirms the problem is a missing capability, not missing guidance. Why not the others: A repeats the prompt change that already had no effect; B defines more subagents that still cannot be invoked without the tool; D is another prompt change that cannot grant a capability the configuration withholds.

bank.q: Your synthesis subagent produces a generic, high-level write-up that never cites the specific sources and figures that the search and analysis subagents returned earlier in the coordinator's conversation. Those results were correct and detailed, and the synthesis prompt only says "Synthesize the findings on the topic". What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
o: Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's history, so the coordinator must include the prior findings explicitly in the synthesis prompt
The synthesis subagent's context window is too small to hold the findings, so it should run on a model with a larger context window
The synthesis subagent's temperature is too high, so the coordinator should lower it to keep the write-up grounded in the findings
The synthesis subagent's `max_tokens` is too low to fit the details, so the coordinator should raise it for synthesis calls only
bank.w: Subagents run with isolated context: they see only what the coordinator puts in their prompt. A prompt that just says "Synthesize the findings" passes no findings at all, so the subagent falls back on generic knowledge; the fix is to include the full prior outputs. Why not the others: B treats a capacity problem that does not exist, since the data was never sent; C changes randomness, not the missing input; D raises the output budget, which cannot supply findings the subagent never received.

bank.q: Audit logs show that in 9% of refund cases your support agent calls `process_refund` without first calling `lookup_order`, so it occasionally refunds ineligible orders that were already refunded or are outside the return window. The system prompt already says to check the order first. Order eligibility is a hard business rule. What MOST reliably enforces it?
o: Strengthen the system prompt so it states in bold, at the top and again at the end, that `lookup_order` must always precede `process_refund`
Add a programmatic gate that rejects `process_refund` unless a successful `lookup_order` result for that order exists in session state
Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing the agent calling `lookup_order` before `process_refund` in several refund cases
Add a routing classifier that enables `process_refund` only for requests it labels as refunds, so other conversations cannot refund
bank.w: A hard business rule needs a deterministic guarantee, and a prerequisite gate in code makes it impossible to refund without a successful lookup for that order. The existing prompt instruction and its 9% failure rate show that guidance alone is not enough. Why not the others: A is the same probabilistic guidance with more emphasis; C is also prompt guidance and keeps a non-zero failure rate; D controls which tools are available for a request, not the order in which they are called.

bank.q: A customer writes one message with three distinct issues: a billing error on last month's invoice, a damaged item from a recent order, and a new shipping address for future orders. Your support agent fixes the billing error, ends its turn, and the customer has to repeat the other two. CSAT on multi-issue chats is 20 points lower. Which workflow design BEST handles this?
o: Reply asking the customer to resubmit each remaining issue as a separate message, so the agent can handle them one at a time
Escalate the conversation to a human, since three simultaneous issues exceed what the agent should handle in a single conversation
Handle exactly one issue per turn and ask the customer to confirm before moving on, so each resolution is acknowledged separately
Split the request into separate issues, investigate each using shared customer context, then reply with one combined resolution
bank.w: Multi-concern requests should be decomposed into distinct items, each investigated with the shared customer context (in parallel where possible), and answered with one unified resolution, which removes the need for the customer to repeat anything. Why not the others: A pushes the decomposition onto the customer, the very friction behind the lower CSAT; B escalates issues the agent can handle; C stretches the conversation over several turns and keeps the disjointed experience.

bank.q: When your support agent escalates a complex billing dispute through `escalate_to_human`, the human agent, who has no access to the chat transcript, receives only "Escalating billing issue". Average handle time for escalated cases is 14 minutes because staff must re-gather everything from the customer. What should the handoff MOST importantly include?
o: The complete raw conversation transcript copied verbatim into the handoff, so the human can read every message the customer sent
A short, polite apology message that the human can forward directly to the customer when they first pick up the escalated case
A structured summary with the customer ID, root-cause analysis, disputed amount and a recommended action for the human to take
The agent's confidence score that escalation was the right decision, along with the number of turns spent before escalating
bank.w: A structured handoff gives a human who cannot see the transcript the facts needed to act immediately: who the customer is, what went wrong, how much is disputed, and what to do next, which removes the re-gathering behind the 14-minute handle time. Why not the others: A dumps an unstructured transcript the human must still digest to find the key facts; B transfers no case information; D describes the agent's own process, not the customer's case.

bank.q: Company policy requires human approval for any refund over $500. Your support agent is told this in its system prompt and asked to self-check before refunding, yet last month it processed four refunds above the limit when the self-check failed. Compliance now requires a guaranteed block. What should you implement?
o: A hook that intercepts `process_refund` calls above $500, blocks them, and redirects the case to the human escalation workflow
A stronger, more explicit system prompt instruction restating the $500 limit and the approval requirement in several places
Few-shot examples in the system prompt that show refunds over $500 being escalated to a human instead of processed by the agent
A check inside `process_refund` that asks the model to confirm the amount is within policy before the refund is executed
bank.w: A tool-call interception hook enforces the limit in code: any `process_refund` above $500 is blocked and redirected to escalation regardless of what the model decides, which is the guarantee compliance asks for. Why not the others: B is more prompt guidance, the same probabilistic mechanism whose self-check already failed four times; C is also guidance, improving the odds without guaranteeing anything; D routes the decision back through the fallible model instead of enforcing the rule.

bank.q: Three MCP tools return dates differently: `get_customer` uses ISO 8601, `lookup_order` uses Unix epoch seconds, and a legacy status tool returns numeric codes. Your support agent misreads them about 15% of the time when reasoning about timelines, such as return windows. Every result must be normalized to one format before the model reasons over it, every time. What is MOST reliable?
o: A system prompt section documenting each tool's date format and instructing the model to convert values before reasoning on them
A `PostToolUse` hook that converts each tool's output to one normalized date format before the model processes the result
Few-shot examples in the system prompt showing the correct interpretation of each of the three formats in timeline questions
A note in `CLAUDE.md` describing the three date formats and the tools that return each one, loaded at the start of every session
bank.w: A `PostToolUse` hook intercepts every tool result and transforms it in code before the model sees it, so normalization happens deterministically on every call, which is exactly the "every time" requirement. Why not the others: A asks the model to do the conversion itself, the probabilistic step behind the 15% misreads; C is also guidance that improves but cannot guarantee interpretation; D is documentation in context, which still relies on the model applying it correctly.

bank.q: Your team wants Claude to review every pull request with the same three steps each time: a lint check, then a security scan, then a test-coverage check, each producing its own section of the report. The steps never change between PRs, and reviewers complain that the current single all-in-one prompt skips checks unpredictably. Which decomposition strategy fits BEST?
o: Dynamic adaptive decomposition, where the agent decides which checks to run next based on what each pass discovers in the PR
Keep a single prompt asking for all three checks at once, adding a checklist so the agent confirms every check before replying
Three parallel subagents, one per check, each posting its own comment on the PR directly with no coordinator merging findings
A fixed sequential pipeline using prompt chaining, running lint, then security, then coverage in the same order on every PR
bank.w: When the steps are predictable and identical on every run, a fixed pipeline built with prompt chaining is the right decomposition: each step gets focused attention and runs in a defined order, so no check is skipped. Why not the others: A is meant for open-ended investigations whose steps are unknown in advance, adding variability the team does not want; B keeps the all-in-one prompt that already skips checks; C produces three disconnected outputs with nothing to merge them into one report.

bank.q: A developer asks your productivity agent to "find and fix the performance bottlenecks in this 200-file service" before a load test on Friday. Nobody knows where the bottlenecks are, and the team has seen that fixing one hotspot often exposes another that was hidden behind it. Which task decomposition strategy fits BEST?
o: A fixed pipeline that opens each of the 200 files once in directory order and applies any optimization it finds along the way
A single prompt instructing the agent to "fix all performance issues now" across the service, then report every change it made
An adaptive plan: profile to find hotspots, fix the highest-impact one, then re-profile and let the next steps follow the results
Parallel subagents, one per file, each optimizing its file independently, with the changes merged together at the end of the run
bank.w: The bottlenecks are unknown and interact, since fixing one can reveal another, so the plan must adapt to intermediate results: profiling locates hotspots, the highest-impact fix comes first, and re-profiling decides what to do next. Why not the others: A follows directory order instead of impact and ignores interactions; B is a single shot that cannot reveal hotspots hidden behind the first fix; D optimizes files in isolation and misses cross-file causes.

bank.q: Yesterday you ran a named codebase-analysis session on the payments module. This morning you continue it with `--resume`, but teammates merged changes to four of the module's files overnight. The agent now answers from its earlier analysis, describing code that no longer exists. You want to keep the still-valid work without building on outdated results. What is the BEST practice?
o: Tell the resumed session which files changed so it re-analyzes them; if most prior context is now invalid, start fresh with a summary
Stop using `--resume` for codebase analysis and start every session from scratch, re-reading the whole module each morning
Keep resuming and trust the prior analysis, since overnight changes to a few files rarely affect the conclusions about a module
Use `fork_session` to branch from yesterday's analysis and continue the investigation in the new branch instead of the old one
bank.w: Resuming is right while context is mostly current, but the agent must be told which files changed so it re-reads them rather than relying on stale tool results; if the changes invalidate most of the analysis, a new session seeded with a structured summary is more reliable. Why not the others: B discards valid work every day; C is the behavior that already produced answers about code that no longer exists; D creates a branch that inherits the same stale baseline.

bank.q: After a long session that built a shared analysis of your billing service's architecture, you want to compare two refactoring approaches, extracting a ledger module or introducing an event bus, side by side. Each exploration must not pollute the other's context, and you do not want to rebuild the baseline analysis twice. Which mechanism fits BEST?
o: Use `--resume` to reopen the same session twice in a row and try one approach after the other within that single conversation
Use `fork_session` to create two independent branches from the shared baseline, explore one approach in each, then compare
Lower the temperature and ask the agent to weigh both refactoring approaches against each other in a single detailed response
Start two new, unrelated sessions, one per approach, and have each one rebuild its own analysis of the billing service first
bank.w: `fork_session` creates independent branches from shared context: both explorations start from the same baseline analysis, and neither sees the other's work, which meets both constraints. Why not the others: A keeps both approaches in one conversation, so the second exploration is shaped by the first; C is a single context and a single answer, not two real explorations; D rebuilds the baseline twice, which you wanted to avoid, and the two analyses may not even match.

bank.q: In your research system, the coordinator hands web-search results to one of two tools, `analyze_content` and `analyze_document`, whose descriptions differ by a single word. About 20% of web results land in `analyze_document`, which expects uploaded files, and its summaries come back malformed. The team wants a low-effort fix that addresses the cause rather than the symptom. What is the MOST effective first step?
o: Add 5–8 few-shot examples to the system prompt showing web results routed to `analyze_content` and uploaded files to `analyze_document`
Add a routing layer that inspects each input before the turn and preselects the tool, based on whether it contains URLs or file IDs
Rename the web tool to `extract_web_results` and rewrite both descriptions so each states a distinct purpose with no overlap
Force `tool_choice` to `analyze_document` whenever a document is attached to the request, and leave the other cases on auto
bank.w: The misrouting comes from two tools whose names and descriptions overlap almost entirely, and descriptions are the model's primary selection signal. Renaming the web tool and rewriting both descriptions to state distinct purposes removes the ambiguity at its source, at low effort. Why not the others: A adds tokens on every request while the overlapping descriptions stay ambiguous; B is infrastructure that bypasses the model's language understanding instead of fixing the cause; D pins a tool by a crude rule and misroutes requests where a document is attached but the web result is what needs analysis.

bank.q: Your support agent's tool descriptions were rewritten last sprint and now clearly separate `get_customer` from `lookup_order`, yet the agent still calls `get_customer` first on 60% of order-only questions such as "where is order #5521?". While reviewing the setup, you notice the system prompt says "always confirm the customer first" in three places. What should you investigate FIRST?
o: The system prompt wording, since keyword-sensitive instructions can create tool associations that override good descriptions
Whether the `get_customer` description has grown too long and should be cut back to a single line so it competes less
Whether `get_customer` and `lookup_order` should be merged into a single `lookup_entity` tool that decides internally
Whether `tool_choice` should be set to "any" so the model is required to pick a tool before writing any reply
bank.w: The descriptions are already clear, so the remaining cause is the repeated instruction in the system prompt: wording like "always confirm the customer first" creates an association with `get_customer` that can override well-written descriptions. Inspecting and rewording the prompt targets that cause directly. Why not the others: B shortening descriptions usually makes selection worse, not better; C is a heavy redesign that removes a useful distinction without touching the prompt; D only forces some tool call, which the agent already makes, and does nothing about which tool it picks.

bank.q: Your developer productivity agent connects to two MCP tools, `search_code` and `lookup_ticket`, described only as "Searches the codebase" and "Looks things up". Questions like "what's the status of PROJ-481?" go to `search_code` about 25% of the time, returning irrelevant code hits. The team wants a fix it can ship today without new components. What is the MOST effective first step?
o: Add a routing layer that detects ticket-ID patterns like `PROJ-481` in the message and preselects `lookup_ticket` before each turn
Merge both tools into a single lookup tool that inspects the input and decides internally whether to query code or tickets
Force `tool_choice` to `lookup_ticket` whenever the user message contains a hyphenated ID, and leave everything else on auto
Expand each description with accepted inputs, example queries, edge cases, and when to use it instead of the other tool
bank.w: One-line descriptions give the model almost nothing to separate two tools, and descriptions are its primary selection mechanism. Enriching them with inputs, example queries, edge cases, and explicit boundaries is a low-effort, high-leverage fix that needs no new components. Why not the others: A adds the component the team wants to avoid and swaps model understanding for pattern matching; B discards a useful distinction and hides the routing inside one overloaded tool; C is a brittle rule that misfires on hyphenated strings that are not tickets, such as branch names or package versions.

bank.q: Your support agent has one `manage_account` tool that updates addresses, changes plans, or closes accounts based on a free-form `action` string. Audits show it picked the wrong action on 3% of calls last month, including two accounts closed when the customer only wanted a plan change. Security also wants to require extra approval for closures only. Which design MOST improves reliability?
o: Add "choose the action carefully and confirm it matches the request" to the `manage_account` description, with one example per action
Split `manage_account` into `update_address`, `change_plan`, and `close_account`, each with its own defined input and output contract
Keep one `manage_account` tool but constrain the `action` argument to an enum of the three allowed values to reject typos
Force `tool_choice` to `manage_account` for every account request so the agent never answers account questions in prose
bank.w: Purpose-specific tools give the model a clear selection signal per action, and separate contracts let each one be validated and permissioned on its own, which is exactly what the extra approval for closures requires. Why not the others: A is vague guidance that leaves the risky multi-purpose design in place; C prevents invalid strings but still routes every action, closures included, through one tool where the wrong valid value can be chosen; D forces the tool to be called but does nothing about which action is selected.

bank.q: When a customer with no purchase history asks about their orders, `lookup_order` returns the same error payload it returns on a database timeout. The agent retries three times, then tells the customer "something went wrong, please try later", and the customer opens a second ticket. Timeouts do still happen a few times a day. What is the BEST fix to the tool's response design?
o: Return a valid empty result (successful query, no matches) distinctly from an access failure such as a timeout that needs a retry decision
Mark every empty result as a transient error with `isRetryable: true`, so the agent treats them exactly like database timeouts
When the current query is empty, fall back to returning the customer's most recent historical order so the agent has something to show
Treat any empty result as a permission error and escalate the conversation to a human agent who can inspect the account directly
bank.w: No orders is a correct answer, not a failure. Returning it as a successful empty result lets the agent tell the customer "no orders found", while real timeouts, which still occur, keep a distinct error shape that supports a retry decision. Why not the others: B makes the pointless retries the default behavior; C returns data that does not answer the question and may mislead the customer; D mislabels a normal outcome as a permission problem and spends human time on it.

bank.q: Your search subagent queries an external academic index that times out on roughly 1 in 30 calls, usually succeeding on a second try. Today any timeout aborts the whole research run, and a run that had already gathered 40 sources was lost this week. The coordinator should stay free of routine recovery work. How should error handling be structured for reliable recovery?
o: Propagate every error to the coordinator immediately, without local retries, so a single component makes all recovery decisions
Catch the timeout inside the subagent and return an empty result marked as successful, so the run continues without interruption
Raise the timeout to a top-level handler that aborts the run cleanly and notifies the user, so no partial report goes out
Retry transient failures inside the subagent, and escalate only unresolved errors with the steps attempted and any partial results
bank.w: Transient timeouts that usually succeed on retry should be recovered locally, which keeps routine work away from the coordinator. When retries do not help, the error goes up with what was attempted and the sources already gathered, so the coordinator can decide without losing progress. Why not the others: A floods the coordinator with routine recovery it should not handle; B suppresses the failure as success, so missing coverage silently corrupts the report; C keeps the current behavior that throws away a whole run over one recoverable timeout.

bank.q: Your MCP tools return every failure as `{"error": "failed"}`. Logs show the agent retrying refund-policy violations that can never succeed, giving up at once on timeouts that would pass on retry, and telling customers "something went wrong" when a search simply has no matches. You can change the tool responses but not the model. Which redesign is MOST effective?
o: Wrap every tool call in a global policy that retries three times with backoff before reporting the failure back to the agent
Log all errors server-side for the on-call team and have the agent apologize to the customer with a single generic message
Return structured errors with an `errorCategory`, an `isRetryable` flag, and a human-readable message for the agent to act on
Map every failure to a transient error so the agent retries consistently and never gives up on a call that might succeed
bank.w: The agent fails in three different ways because one generic error hides what happened. An `errorCategory` (transient, validation, business, permission) plus `isRetryable` lets it retry timeouts, stop on policy violations and explain them, and the message gives it wording for the customer; empty searches then need not be reported as errors at all. Why not the others: A wastes calls retrying policy violations that can never pass; B throws away the signal the agent needs to recover; D labels everything transient, which guarantees futile retries on business errors.

bank.q: In your research pipeline, `extract_metadata` must run before any of the four enrichment tools, because they need its output. With `tool_choice: "auto"` and a system prompt instruction to call it first, logs show an enrichment tool going first in about 6% of runs, producing incomplete records. You need a guarantee, not a higher success rate. How should you configure the call?
o: Keep `tool_choice: "auto"` and list `extract_metadata` first among the tool definitions so the model sees it before the others
Force `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` on the first turn, then run enrichment in follow-up turns
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first turn so the model is required to call a tool before it writes any text response
Strengthen the system prompt with a numbered procedure that puts `extract_metadata` first, repeated at the end of the user message
bank.w: Forced tool selection makes the model call exactly the named tool, so `extract_metadata` runs first by construction; enrichment proceeds in later turns once its output exists. Why not the others: A relies on definition order, which does not control which tool the model picks; C guarantees that some tool is called, not which one, so an enrichment tool can still go first; D is still prompt guidance, the same probabilistic approach that already fails in 6% of runs.

bank.q: Your document analysis subagent was given a generic `fetch_url` tool to download source PDFs. Reviews show it also pulls blog posts, forum threads, and news pages that are irrelevant to the documents it was asked to analyze, adding noise to its findings. It still needs to fetch the documents themselves. What is the BEST constraint to apply?
o: Replace `fetch_url` with a constrained `load_document` tool that validates document URLs and rejects anything else
Give every subagent the same `fetch_url` tool, so URL handling stays consistent across roles and is easier to monitor
Remove all tools from the subagent and have the coordinator fetch every document and pass the content in the prompt
Keep `fetch_url` but add a system prompt rule listing the domains the subagent is not allowed to visit
bank.w: The subagent needs to fetch documents, not arbitrary pages, so the tool itself should express that boundary: a `load_document` tool that validates document URLs keeps the needed capability while making off-target fetches fail at the interface. Why not the others: B spreads the same overly broad capability to more agents; C strips a capability the subagent legitimately needs and pushes extra work onto the coordinator; D is a fragile denylist in the prompt that cannot anticipate every irrelevant domain and is not enforced.

bank.q: Each of your four research subagents (search, analysis, synthesis, report) was given all 16 tools "for flexibility". Since then, the synthesis subagent sometimes launches web searches and the search subagent tries to write reports. One teammate suggests a bigger reasoning budget, another merging the subagents. The synthesis subagent does need quick fact checks often. Which fix is BEST?
o: Keep all 16 tools on every subagent but add detailed few-shot examples per role showing which tools that role should use
Raise each subagent's reasoning budget so it can deliberate more carefully over all 16 tools before each selection
Merge the four subagents into one agent that holds all 16 tools, so there is a single place where tool choice happens
Scope each subagent to the tools its role needs, plus at most one narrow cross-role tool for a frequent need like fact checks
bank.w: Too many tools, and tools outside a role's specialization, degrade selection; 16 is far above the handful that works well. Scoping each subagent to its role removes the wrong choices entirely, and one narrow cross-role tool covers the synthesis subagent's frequent fact checks. Why not the others: A keeps the same decision complexity and only adds guidance; B treats a tool-overload problem as a capacity problem; C makes the overload worse by putting every tool and every role in one agent.

bank.q: Your extraction pipeline offers three tools, `extract_invoice`, `extract_receipt`, and `extract_contract`. About 2% of the time Claude replies with a chatty summary instead of calling any tool, and the downstream parser crashes. Batches mix all three document types, and the type is not known before the call. Which `tool_choice` setting BEST guarantees structured output?
o: `tool_choice: "auto"`, letting the model decide for each document in the batch whether a tool call is needed at all
`tool_choice: "any"`, so the model must call one of the three tools but still chooses which one fits the document
Force `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}` for every document, as invoices are most common
Keep the default setting and add "always use a tool, never reply in prose" to the system prompt and the user message
bank.w: `tool_choice: "any"` requires a tool call, which eliminates the prose replies, while still letting the model pick the schema that matches each document, which matters because the type is unknown in advance. Why not the others: A is the current behavior that allows prose replies; C guarantees a tool call but forces the invoice schema onto receipts and contracts; D is a prompt instruction, which lowers the rate but does not guarantee a tool call.

bank.q: Your team's productivity agent spends its first 6 to 10 tool calls on every task searching Jira to discover which issues exist before it can act, adding latency and cost. The issue summaries change a few times a day. A teammate proposes pasting the full issue list into the system prompt. Which MCP mechanism BEST gives the agent up-front visibility into the available issues?
o: Add several more granular Jira search tools, such as by label and by assignee, so each exploratory search returns faster
Paste the full list of issue summaries into the system prompt on every request, regenerated by a script every hour
Expose the issue summaries as an MCP resource, a content catalog the agent can see without exploratory tool calls
Add a `list_all_issues` tool and instruct the agent to call it at the start of every turn before doing anything else
bank.w: MCP resources exist to expose content catalogs such as issue summaries, so the agent knows what data is available without spending tool calls exploring for it. Why not the others: A adds more tools, which makes each search narrower but does not remove the exploration itself; B spends context on the entire list in every request and goes stale between regenerations; D replaces exploration with a mandatory call on every turn, which is rigid and still wasteful.

bank.q: Your team wants Claude Code to read and update Jira issues: search, comment, and transition status, the standard operations. One engineer estimates three weeks to build a custom MCP server for full control, yet nothing in the workflow is specific to your company. The team wants the integration this sprint. What is the MOST appropriate choice?
o: Use an existing community MCP server for the standard Jira operations, and reserve custom servers for team-specific workflows
Build the custom MCP server for full control over every operation, accepting the three-week cost as a long-term investment
Skip MCP for now and have developers paste the relevant Jira issue data into the conversation manually when they need it
Use the built-in `Grep` tool against the saved HTML of the Jira web UI to find issue text without any extra integration
bank.w: For a standard integration with nothing company-specific, an existing community MCP server delivers it this sprint; custom servers are worth their cost only for genuinely team-specific workflows. Why not the others: B spends three weeks reproducing standard functionality for no added value; C abandons automation and leaves developers doing manual copy and paste; D misuses `Grep`, which searches local file contents and cannot update issues.

bank.q: You are trying a brand-new, unstable MCP server on your own machine and do not want it to reach teammates or the repo. Separately, the team's stable GitHub MCP server should be available to everyone who clones the repo, authenticated with a token that must never be committed. How should you configure the two servers?
o: Put both servers in the project-scoped `.mcp.json`, so all MCP configuration lives in one reviewed place in the repo
Put both servers in each developer's `~/.claude.json`, so every developer controls their own setup independently
Put the GitHub server in `.mcp.json` with the token written inline, and describe the experimental one in `CLAUDE.md`
Experimental server in your user-scoped `~/.claude.json`; GitHub server in `.mcp.json` with `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` for the token
bank.w: Personal and experimental servers belong in user scope (`~/.claude.json`), where they affect only you. Team servers belong in the project-scoped `.mcp.json` shared through the repo, and environment variable expansion such as `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` keeps the secret out of version control. Why not the others: A ships the unstable server to every teammate; B means the team server is not shared through the repo and each developer must set it up by hand; C commits the secret, and `CLAUDE.md` holds instructions, it does not configure MCP servers.

bank.q: Before a refactor of the payments module, a developer asks your agent for two things: (1) every test file matching `**/*.test.tsx` across the monorepo, and (2) every place that calls `processPayment`. The repo has about 3,000 files, and the agent should not spend context reading files it does not need. Which built-in tools fit each task, respectively?
o: `Grep` for both tasks, searching for `.test.tsx` in file contents first and then for the `processPayment` call sites
`Glob` for the file-name pattern search, and `Grep` for finding the callers of `processPayment` inside file contents
`Glob` for both tasks, matching the test file pattern first and then file names that contain `processPayment`
`Bash` with `ls` for the test files, and `Read` on each source file to look for calls to `processPayment`
bank.w: `Glob` matches file paths by name or extension pattern, which is exactly the test file question, while `Grep` searches inside file contents, which is how call sites of a function are found without reading whole files. Why not the others: A searches contents for something that lives in file names; C matches names, but callers of a function live inside the code; D is slower, less reliable, and reading every file wastes the context the agent should save.

bank.q: Your agent is updating a config loader and its `Edit` call fails: the target line `timeout = 30` appears in four places in the file, so there is no unique match. The agent has retried the identical edit twice with the same error. The file is 120 lines long and its other recent changes must be preserved exactly. What is the MOST reliable fallback?
o: Keep retrying the same `Edit` call with the same anchor text, since intermittent tool errors often clear on a later attempt
Use `Grep` to locate every occurrence of `timeout = 30` and replace the right one in place directly from the search results
Use `Read` to load the full file, then `Write` the modified contents, the fallback for when `Edit` has no unique anchor
Delete the file with `Bash` and recreate it from memory with `Write`, including the corrected timeout on the right line
bank.w: When `Edit` cannot find a unique anchor, `Read` loads the exact current contents and `Write` saves the full modified file, so the change lands on the intended line and every other line is preserved. Why not the others: A repeats a deterministic failure that has already happened twice; B misunderstands `Grep`, which searches file contents but cannot edit them; D rebuilds the file from memory, risking lost or fabricated lines in a file whose other changes must be kept exactly.

bank.q: A developer asks your productivity agent to explain how authentication flows through an unfamiliar 500-file service before a security review tomorrow. On a first attempt, the agent began reading files one by one and exhausted its context window before reaching the session-handling code, without producing an answer. Which use of the built-in tools is MOST effective for this task?
o: `Read` every file in the repository once, in directory order, so the agent builds a complete picture before answering anything
Use `Glob` to list every source file, then `Read` them alphabetically, summarizing each one into a running notes file as it goes
Have the agent describe a typical authentication flow from general knowledge, then confirm it against two or three files
`Grep` for entry points such as the auth middleware, then `Read` selectively to follow imports, expanding only as needed
bank.w: Codebase understanding should be built incrementally: `Grep` locates the entry points, and `Read` follows imports from those anchors, so context is spent only on the files on the authentication path. Why not the others: A is the strategy that already exhausted the context window; B is still a read-everything approach, merely reordered, and the notes do not reduce the reading cost; C starts from generic assumptions instead of this codebase, and spot-checking a few files cannot validate a flow the agent never traced.

bank.q: Your monorepo's root `CLAUDE.md` has grown past 900 lines of standards for twelve packages, and maintainers complain that the payments package gets loaded with mobile UI rules it never needs. Each package team wants only its relevant standards in context, and shared standards must stay in version control, maintained in one place. What is the cleanest approach?
o: Keep the single root `CLAUDE.md` with one heading per package and rely on Claude to find the section that applies to each package
Move all of the standards into the user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` so the repository root stays short and easy to navigate
Delete every standard that does not apply to all twelve packages, keeping only the universal rules in the root `CLAUDE.md`
Split standards into separate files and have each package's `CLAUDE.md` pull in only the relevant ones with `@path` imports
bank.w: Importing files with `@path` (e.g., `@./standards/api.md`) keeps `CLAUDE.md` modular: shared standards live once in version control, and each package's `CLAUDE.md` pulls in only the files it needs, so the payments package no longer carries mobile UI rules. Why not the others: A keeps every package's context bloated and relies on inference to pick the right section; B moves team standards to a user-level file that is not shared through version control; C discards legitimate package-specific standards instead of scoping them.

bank.q: Developers on your team report that Claude Code follows the repo's logging conventions in some sessions and ignores them in others, even within the same package. You suspect a stray directory-level `CLAUDE.md` or a personal memory file is loading, or that the expected one is not. Before changing any file, you want evidence of what is actually in effect. What is the BEST first step?
o: Delete every `CLAUDE.md` in the repository and rebuild them from scratch so you know exactly which instructions exist
Run the `/memory` command in an affected session to verify which memory files are actually loaded and where they come from
Restart Claude Code several times in the affected package until the behavior stabilizes, then compare the sessions' output
Consolidate everything into one root `CLAUDE.md` and assume that file is the one that loads, removing the other locations
bank.w: `/memory` shows which memory files are loaded in the current session, which is exactly the evidence the team wants before anything is changed; it reveals a stray directory-level file or a missing project file directly. Why not the others: A is destructive guesswork that changes files before diagnosing; C is trial and error that never shows which files are active; D assumes rather than verifies, and throws away legitimate structure without knowing the cause.

bank.q: You wrote your team's coding standards into `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, and Claude Code follows them perfectly on your laptop. A contractor who cloned the repository yesterday, running the same Claude Code version, reports that Claude ignores the standards entirely. The standards must reach the contractor and every future hire without manual setup. What is the cause, and what is the BEST fix?
o: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is user-level and not version-controlled; move the standards to the project-level `CLAUDE.md` to share them
The contractor's Claude Code installation is outdated and cannot read the standards; upgrading it will load them on next start
The contractor must run `/memory` to load your `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` manually, then repeat it at the start of each session
Directory-level files override user-level ones, so the standards must be copied into a `CLAUDE.md` in every subdirectory
bank.w: Instructions in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` are user-scoped: they apply only on your machine and never travel with the repository. Moving them to the project-level `CLAUDE.md` (root or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`) puts them under version control, so the contractor and future hires get them on clone. Why not the others: B is ruled out because both run the same version; C misreads `/memory`, which inspects loaded memory files and cannot reach another user's home directory; D is false, and duplicating standards into every subdirectory creates drift.

bank.q: Your security team turned its review checklist into a `/security-review` slash command, and today it exists only on the lead's laptop. Leadership wants every developer to get the command automatically when they clone or pull the repository, with changes reviewed through normal pull requests. Nobody should need a per-machine setup step. Where should the command file live?
o: In `~/.claude/commands/` in each developer's home directory, distributed through the onboarding script for new laptops
In `.claude/commands/` inside the project repository, so it is version-controlled and arrives with every clone or pull
In the project root `CLAUDE.md` under a "Commands" heading that spells out each step of the security checklist
In a `.claude/config.json` file with a commands array that registers `/security-review` for the whole project
bank.w: Project-scoped commands live in `.claude/commands/` in the repository, so they are version-controlled, reviewed through pull requests, and available to everyone after a clone or pull with no per-machine setup. Why not the others: A is user scope, which needs exactly the per-machine step that leadership rules out; C puts context in `CLAUDE.md`, which does not define a slash command; D describes a `.claude/config.json` mechanism that does not exist for defining commands.

bank.q: Your developer productivity team ships an `/audit-dependencies` skill that walks the dependency tree and prints several hundred lines of output. After running it mid-task, developers find Claude has lost track of the bug they were fixing, because the audit output crowded the earlier context out. The audit must keep its full depth. Which `SKILL.md` frontmatter setting BEST addresses this?
o: `allowed-tools`, restricting the skill to read-only tools so the audit cannot touch files while it walks the tree
`argument-hint`, prompting for a package name at invocation so each run audits a narrower slice of the tree
`context: fork`, running the skill in an isolated subagent context so its verbose output stays out of the main session
No frontmatter change; move the skill to `~/.claude/skills/` so it only runs for developers who explicitly opt in
bank.w: `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated subagent context, so hundreds of lines of dependency output never enter the main conversation and the bug-fix context survives, while the audit keeps its full depth. Why not the others: A restricts tools, which is a safety control and does nothing about output volume; B narrows the scope, which conflicts with keeping the audit's full depth; D only changes who has the skill, and anyone who runs it still floods their session.

bank.q: Your `/deploy` skill needs a target environment name such as `staging` or `prod`. In the last month, a third of invocations came without one, and the skill failed halfway after guessing. A teammate added a reminder to the project `CLAUDE.md`, but developers still forget. You want the skill itself to prompt for the missing parameter. Which `SKILL.md` frontmatter option fits?
o: `argument-hint`, which prompts developers for the required environment parameter when they invoke the skill without it
`context: fork`, which runs the deployment in an isolated subagent context so a failed run does not affect the session
`allowed-tools`, which limits the skill to the deployment tools so it cannot guess an environment from other sources
A stronger note in the project `CLAUDE.md` telling developers to always pass the environment name after `/deploy`
bank.w: `argument-hint` is the frontmatter option that prompts developers for required parameters at invocation, so the missing environment name is requested by the skill itself rather than guessed. Why not the others: B isolates the skill's context but does nothing about the missing argument; C restricts tool access, which is unrelated to input; D is the reminder approach that already failed, since prose guidance in `CLAUDE.md` does not request input from anyone.

bank.q: Your team's `/reorganize-files` skill moves and rewrites files to match a new folder layout. Twice this month it ran destructive Bash commands, once deleting a generated directory that was not in version control. The skill must stay available to the whole team, but during execution it should only be able to perform file-write operations. Which frontmatter option BEST fits?
o: `context: fork`, so the skill runs in an isolated subagent context and its actions stay out of the main conversation
`argument-hint`, so developers must name the target folders explicitly before the skill is allowed to start moving files
No frontmatter change; move the skill to `~/.claude/skills/` so only the lead can run it and review each command first
`allowed-tools`, restricting the skill's tool access to file-write operations so it cannot run destructive Bash commands
bank.w: `allowed-tools` restricts which tools the skill can use, so limiting it to file-write operations removes Bash and enforces the constraint during execution, while the skill stays available to the team. bank.q: Your team has two kinds of guidance: naming and formatting standards that every interaction must follow, and a 14-step release checklist used about twice a month. Today both sit in `CLAUDE.md`, and developers notice the checklist inflating context in every session, even routine bug fixes. The standards must never be skipped. How should each be configured?
o: Keep both in `CLAUDE.md`, moving the release checklist to the bottom of the file so it is always available when needed
Move both into skills so each one loads only when it is needed, keeping the context of everyday sessions minimal
Keep the universal standards in `CLAUDE.md`, which always loads, and move the release checklist into an on-demand skill
Move the universal standards into a skill and keep the release checklist in `CLAUDE.md`, where it is easier to find
bank.w: `CLAUDE.md` is loaded in every session, which suits standards that must never be skipped, while skills are invoked on demand, which suits a checklist used twice a month and removes it from routine sessions. Why not the others: A keeps inflating every session's context, which is the problem described; B makes the always-required standards optional, since they would load only when invoked; D inverts the two, leaving universal standards on demand and the rare checklist always loaded.

bank.q: Your test files (`*.test.ts`) are spread across 60+ directories in the monorepo, and all of them must follow the same mocking and naming conventions. Today the conventions live in the root `CLAUDE.md`, and Claude applies them only some of the time. New test directories appear every sprint, and nobody wants to maintain per-directory files. What is the MOST maintainable way to apply them automatically?
o: A `.claude/rules/` file with frontmatter `paths: ["**/*.test.ts"]`, so the rule loads whenever a matching file is edited
A separate `CLAUDE.md` in every directory that contains test files, added by a script whenever a new test directory appears
Keep the conventions in the root `CLAUDE.md` under a bold heading and rely on Claude to infer when they should apply
A `/test-conventions` skill that developers are asked to invoke before they start editing any of the test files
bank.w: A rule in `.claude/rules/` with a `paths` glob such as `**/*.test.ts` loads by file type regardless of directory, so new test directories are covered automatically with a single file to maintain. Why not the others: B is directory-bound and is exactly the per-directory maintenance the team wants to avoid; C is the current setup, which relies on inference and applies conventions inconsistently; D depends on developers remembering to invoke it, so it is not automatic.

bank.q: Your team must migrate an internal HTTP client to a new vendor SDK. The change touches 45+ files across three services, and two viable approaches exist, a thin adapter layer or rewriting every call site, each with different infrastructure and rollback implications. Nobody has committed to an approach, and the tech lead wants a decision before any code is edited. How should you use Claude Code?
o: Use direct execution with one comprehensive upfront instruction that specifies every change file by file, leaving nothing to chance
Start in plan mode to explore the call sites, compare both approaches and their implications, and agree on a design before any edits
Use direct execution on the first service, and switch to plan mode only if problems surface partway through the implementation
Spawn parallel subagents that each implement one approach end to end on a separate branch, then compare the finished results
bank.w: Plan mode fits large-scale changes with multiple valid approaches and architectural implications: Claude explores the codebase and designs before committing to edits, which is exactly what the tech lead asked for. Why not the others: A assumes the right structure is already known, when the approach has not even been chosen; C ignores complexity that is known up front and invites costly rework; D builds two full implementations of a 45-file change before any design decision, wasting effort that a plan would avoid.

bank.q: A bug report includes a clear stack trace pointing to an off-by-one error in `paginate()` inside a single file: the last page is always dropped. The fix is a one-character change, the cause is fully understood, and a regression test already reproduces it. A teammate suggests starting in plan mode, as the team does for every change. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
o: Plan mode, so Claude can design and compare alternative fixes before touching the code, as the team does for every change
Spawn the Explore subagent to map the entire codebase first, in case other callers depend on the off-by-one behavior
Plan mode, then ask Claude for three candidate fixes and pick the one with the smallest diff before applying it
Direct execution, since the change is single-file, well scoped and fully understood, so planning would only add overhead
bank.w: Direct execution fits simple, well-understood changes: a clear stack trace, a single file, a known cause and a test that already reproduces the bug leave nothing to explore or design, so plan mode would only add overhead. Why not the others: A applies plan mode by habit to a change with no alternatives worth comparing; B spends an exploration pass on a trivial, localized fix; C over-applies plan mode and invents alternatives for a one-character change.

bank.q: During a three-phase refactor, Claude's discovery phase lists every use of a deprecated config loader, and the output runs to thousands of lines. By the time discovery ends, the main context is nearly full and Claude starts forgetting decisions agreed earlier in the session. Discovery must still be thorough, and the later phases need those decisions. What BEST preserves the main conversation context?
o: Re-read all relevant files in the main conversation at the start of each phase so nothing discovered earlier is lost
Skip the discovery phase and have Claude work from its assumptions about where the config loader is usually called
Use the Explore subagent for discovery so the verbose output stays isolated and only a summary returns to the main session
Run each phase in a fresh session with no shared context, so discovery output never competes with the later phases
bank.w: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in its own context and returns only a summary, so the main conversation keeps the earlier decisions while discovery stays thorough. Why not the others: A adds even more content to a main context that is already filling up; B gives up thoroughness and works from guesses; D drops the agreed decisions that the later phases need, trading one context problem for a continuity problem.

bank.q: You asked Claude Code to write a function that converts legacy order records into the new billing format, describing the mapping in three paragraphs of prose. Across four runs, Claude produced four different shapes: currency sometimes nested, discounts sometimes merged into totals. The rules themselves are settled; Claude keeps reading them differently. What MOST reliably communicates the expected transformation?
o: Provide 2–3 concrete input and output examples showing legacy records and the exact billing records they should become
Rewrite the prose description to be longer and more detailed, spelling out each rule for the currency and discount fields
Ask Claude to restate the requirements in its own words before implementing, then correct any misunderstanding
Convert the three paragraphs into a numbered list of the same rules so each instruction is easier to follow
bank.w: Concrete input and output examples pin down the exact target shape, including where currency is nested and how discounts are kept, which removes the ambiguity that prose leaves open across runs. Why not the others: B is still prose, so it keeps the interpretation problem and adds more text to misread; C checks understanding of the prose but does not define the mapping itself; D reformats the same instructions without making them any less ambiguous.

bank.q: You need a `rolloverDate()` function for billing cycles that must handle month ends, leap years, time zones and daylight saving changes. Claude's first two attempts looked correct, but each failed a different edge case in staging. Correctness matters more than speed here, and you want a repeatable way to know when the function is actually done. What is the MOST effective way to drive Claude toward it?
o: Describe every edge case in detail in prose, then ask Claude to handle all of them carefully in a single implementation
Write a test suite covering expected behavior and edge cases first, then iterate by sharing the failing tests with Claude
Ask Claude to implement it again, then inspect each output by hand against the edge cases you remember from staging
Raise the model's reasoning effort for this task and accept the first implementation it produces with that setting
bank.w: Test-driven iteration fits edge-case-heavy work: a test suite written first defines done in a repeatable way, and sharing the failing tests gives Claude precise, actionable feedback on each iteration. Why not the others: A is prose, which already failed to pin down every case; C relies on manual inspection, which is slow and depends on remembering the edge cases; D may improve a single attempt but provides no verification that the result is correct.

bank.q: You're asking Claude Code to add a caching layer in front of an inventory service your team inherited last month. You know the basic read path but suspect you have not thought through invalidation, behavior when the service is down, or concurrent writes. Implementation starts next sprint, and you want those gaps surfaced before any code exists. Which technique is BEST?
o: Tell Claude to implement its best guess at the cache now, then fix the issues that surface during next sprint's testing
Write a longer and more detailed prose spec up front, covering everything you currently know about the read path
Ask Claude to implement it with extensive comments explaining every assumption it made, then review those comments
Use the interview pattern: have Claude ask you questions that surface considerations you have not anticipated yet
bank.w: The interview pattern has Claude ask questions before implementing, which surfaces considerations such as invalidation, failure modes and concurrency that you may not have anticipated, before any code exists. Why not the others: A skips the surfacing step and discovers the gaps through defects; B can only contain what you already know, so it cannot reveal your blind spots; C documents assumptions after the code is written instead of eliciting unknowns beforehand.

bank.q: A code review left five issues: a typo in a docstring, a missing import, an unclear log message, a refactor that changes the signature of `calculateFees()`, and an update to its only caller. The refactor and the caller update must stay consistent, while the other three are unrelated to anything else. You want the fixes done correctly with minimal back-and-forth. How should you direct them?
o: Fix all five strictly one at a time in separate messages, keeping every change as small and reviewable as possible
Put all five issues into a single message regardless of how they relate, so Claude handles everything in one pass
Send the refactor and caller update together in one detailed message; handle the three independent fixes in any order
Fix the refactor and the caller update in separate messages, so each change stays isolated and easy to review
bank.w: Interacting issues belong in one message so Claude can keep the new signature of `calculateFees()` and its only caller consistent, while independent issues can be handled sequentially or in any order. Why not the others: A over-splits and separates the interacting pair, risking a broken intermediate state; B over-batches unrelated work with the coupled change and makes each fix harder to verify; D separates the two changes that depend on each other.

bank.q: Your GitHub Actions step runs `claude "Review this PR for security issues"`. The step never finishes and is killed by the 60-minute job timeout; logs show Claude Code waiting for interactive input. A teammate proposes piping `/dev/null` into stdin. You want a documented way to run Claude Code unattended that prints the result and exits. What is the correct fix?
o: Add the `-p` (`--print`) flag so Claude Code runs non-interactively, prints its result to stdout and then exits
Set the environment variable `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` before the command so Claude Code skips the interactive prompts
Pipe `/dev/null` into stdin so Claude Code receives end-of-input immediately instead of waiting for keyboard input
Add a `--batch` flag to the command so Claude Code processes the prompt in batch mode and exits when finished
bank.w: The `-p` (`--print`) flag is the documented non-interactive mode: Claude Code processes the prompt, prints the result and exits, which is exactly what an unattended CI step needs. Why not the others: B relies on an environment variable that is not a Claude Code feature; C is the teammate's workaround, which only masks the symptom and does not put Claude Code in non-interactive mode; D invents a `--batch` flag that does not exist.

bank.q: Your CI review step runs Claude Code with `-p` and produces useful findings, but the pipeline must post each one as an inline PR comment. Today a script parses the prose output, and about one run in ten breaks it when the wording changes. The team needs file, line and severity for every finding in a form the script can rely on. Beyond `-p`, what is the BEST change?
o: Increase the output length allowed for the review so each finding includes more surrounding detail for the parser
Ask Claude in the review prompt to "format the output as JSON" with file, line and severity keys for each finding
Harden the parsing script with regular expressions that cover the phrasings seen in the last month of runs
Add `--output-format json` together with `--json-schema` so the findings are emitted as structured, parseable data
bank.w: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` makes Claude Code emit structured findings that match a schema with file, line and severity, so the posting script no longer depends on wording. Why not the others: A adds more prose without making it structured; B is a prompt request that is not enforced, so malformed or wrapped output can still break the script; C keeps parsing natural language, which stays fragile whenever the phrasing changes again.

bank.q: Your CI pipeline has Claude Code generate a fix for a failing test and then, in the same session, review the change before opening a PR. Over two months, human reviewers caught 23 bugs in these PRs that the self-review never flagged. A teammate proposes adding a second self-review pass in the same session. Which design MOST effectively improves review quality?
o: Have the same session review its output a second time, with an explicit prompt to look harder for its own mistakes
Review with an independent Claude instance that lacks the generator's reasoning context and sees only the change
Enable extended thinking in the generating session before its review step so it reasons more deeply about the change
Increase the generating session's verbosity so it explains each decision in more detail during the review step
bank.w: A session that wrote the code carries its own reasoning and is less likely to question its own decisions; an independent instance without that context reviews the change fresh and catches more of what the generator missed. Why not the others: A is the teammate's proposal and repeats the same blind spot in the same context; C deepens reasoning but keeps the generation bias that caused the misses; D adds explanation, which tends to justify the existing decisions rather than challenge them.

bank.q: Your nightly CI step asks Claude Code to generate tests for recently changed modules. Reviewers reject about half of them: many duplicate scenarios already covered, and most build data by hand instead of using the shared fixtures in `tests/fixtures/`. Rejected tests waste reviewer time every morning. Which change MOST improves the quality of the generated tests?
o: Run the generation step twice each night and keep whichever run produced the larger number of tests for review
Switch to a model with a larger context window and pass the entire repository into every generation run
Document testing standards and available fixtures in `CLAUDE.md`, and provide existing test files in context
Delete the existing tests for each changed module before generating, so there is nothing left to duplicate
bank.w: Documenting testing standards and the shared fixtures in `CLAUDE.md` gives CI-run Claude Code the conventions it was missing, and including existing test files shows which scenarios are already covered, addressing both causes of rejection. Why not the others: A increases volume without addressing duplication or fixture use; B adds raw context but still lacks guidance on which fixtures and standards to use; D destroys valid coverage just to hide duplicates.

bank.q: Your CI review bot posts findings in five categories. The "possible performance issue" category is wrong about 60% of the time, and survey responses show developers now dismiss every bot comment, including accurate security findings. Rewriting the performance prompt properly will take about two weeks. What is the BEST immediate action?
o: Keep every category enabled and ask developers to read each comment carefully while the performance prompt is reworked
Temporarily disable the performance category while you improve its prompt, keeping the accurate categories posting
Add "only report high-confidence performance issues" to that category's prompt, so it posts fewer speculative comments
Have the model attach a confidence score to each performance finding and suppress those that score below 0.7
bank.w: A category with a high false-positive rate erodes trust in every finding, including accurate ones, and the real fix is two weeks away. Disabling it temporarily stops the erosion now, while the accurate categories keep delivering value. Why not the others: A lets trust keep eroding for two more weeks; C is a vague instruction that does not define what counts as high confidence, so precision barely changes; D relies on self-reported confidence, which is poorly calibrated and cannot be trusted as a filter.

bank.q: Your CI reviewer labels severity inconsistently: an unparameterized SQL query is "critical" in one PR and "minor" in another with identical code. The prompt currently says "assign severity (critical, major, minor) based on impact." Release managers gate deployments on critical findings, so labels must be reproducible. Which change MOST improves consistency?
o: Instruct the model to "use good judgment and consider real-world impact carefully" when assigning each severity label
Ask the model to self-report its confidence in each severity label and re-review any label rated below high confidence
Run three independent review passes on every PR and report the average severity across the three for each finding
Define explicit criteria for each severity level, each illustrated with a concrete code example of a finding at that level
bank.w: Inconsistent labels come from an undefined scale: "based on impact" leaves each run to invent its own threshold. Explicit criteria per level, anchored by concrete code examples, give the model a fixed reference, so identical code gets the same label. Why not the others: A is even vaguer than the current prompt; B relies on self-reported confidence, which is poorly calibrated and does not define the levels; C averages labels that are still undefined, adding cost while hiding rather than fixing the inconsistency.

bank.q: Your CI review prompt says "be conservative and only surface high-confidence issues," yet developers still receive dozens of comments per PR on naming and bracket placement, which the linter already handles. The team wants the bot to focus on what the linter cannot catch, without losing real bugs. Which prompt change MOST improves precision?
o: Replace the vague guidance with explicit categories to report, such as bugs and security, and ones to skip, such as style
Strengthen the existing guidance by adding "be even more conservative" and "report only critical issues" to the prompt
Ask the model to rate its confidence in each finding from 1 to 10, and post only findings that it rates 8 or higher
Cap the number of findings the model may return per file at three, so only the most important comments are posted
bank.w: "Conservative" and "high-confidence" do not tell the model which issue types matter. Explicit categorical criteria (report correctness and security, skip subjective style the linter already covers) remove the noise without suppressing real bugs. Why not the others: B adds more of the same vague guidance that has already failed; C uses self-rated confidence, a poorly calibrated proxy; D is an arbitrary cap that can drop real bugs while still posting style comments.

bank.q: Your pipeline extracts metadata from academic papers and returns null for the required `author` field on about 12% of documents. Manual review shows that every one of them lists its authors in a bibliography section rather than inline under the title; the data is present. A teammate proposes relaxing the schema. Which change MOST improves extraction for these documents?
o: Make the `author` field optional, so a null result is accepted by the schema and these documents stop failing validation
Add a prompt instruction stating "the author is always present in the document, so search carefully until you find it"
Add few-shot examples showing correct author extraction from documents with varied layouts, inline and in a bibliography
