Reject documents that do not list authors inline under the title, and route them to a manual data-entry queue instead
bank.w: The information is present but structured differently from what the model expects. Few-shot examples covering both layouts, inline and bibliography, show it where to look and how to extract, which is exactly the gap. Why not the others: A is the teammate's proposal and hides the bug by accepting null for data that exists; B asserts the field exists without demonstrating the pattern, and can push the model to fabricate; D rejects valid documents and moves 12% of the work to humans.

bank.q: Your CI review prompt has three paragraphs describing the finding format: file and line, issue, severity, suggested fix. Output still varies run to run: sometimes a paragraph, sometimes a bullet, and about a third of findings omit the fix. A script turns findings into PR comments and breaks on each variation. What MOST reliably produces a consistent finding format?
o: Add two or three targeted few-shot examples showing complete findings in the exact format, with location, issue and fix
Expand the prose description of the format with stricter wording, and repeat it at the end of the prompt for emphasis
Lower the temperature to 0 so that the model produces more uniform output across runs for the same kind of finding
Increase `max_tokens` so that long findings are never cut off before the suggested fix at the end can be written out
bank.w: Few-shot examples are the most effective way to obtain consistently formatted output: a concrete demonstration of a complete finding is followed far more reliably than prose that has already proven ambiguous. Why not the others: B adds more of the prose instructions that are already failing; C reduces randomness but does not define the structure, so findings can still diverge; D addresses truncation, while the variation described is in structure and omitted fields, not cut-off output.

bank.q: Your CI reviewer keeps flagging a pattern your team uses on purpose: an empty catch block with a logging comment around optional telemetry calls. Developers dismiss about 30 such comments per week. Elsewhere, genuinely swallowed exceptions in payment code have caused real bugs. You want fewer false positives while keeping the model's judgment on novel issues. What is MOST effective?
o: Add a hard rule to the prompt stating "never flag empty catch blocks," so the accepted pattern stops generating comments
Disable the bug-detection category until the prompt can be reworked, keeping only security and style categories active
Tell the model to "use good judgment about what our team considers acceptable" before flagging error-handling code
Add few-shot examples contrasting the accepted telemetry pattern with genuinely swallowed exceptions, explaining each
bank.w: Contrastive few-shot examples show the model why the telemetry pattern is acceptable and why a swallowed payment exception is not, so it generalizes the distinction to new code instead of applying a blanket rule. Why not the others: A is over-broad and would also silence the real bugs in payment code; B throws away all bug detection to fix one pattern; C is vague guidance that does not tell the model what the team actually accepts, so behavior will not change reliably.

bank.q: Your extraction service receives invoices, receipts and bank statements through one endpoint and has a separate extraction tool for each, with its own JSON schema. The document type is not known in advance. Roughly 3% of responses currently come back as plain-text summaries, which the loader cannot ingest. Which `tool_choice` configuration is MOST appropriate?
o: `tool_choice: "auto"`, leaving the model free to decide whether to call one of the extraction tools or answer in text
`tool_choice: "any"`, so the model must call one of the extraction tools but chooses which schema fits the document
Force the invoice extraction tool on every request, since invoices make up most of the traffic reaching the endpoint
Omit `tool_choice` entirely and instruct the model in the system prompt to always return JSON matching one schema
bank.w: `tool_choice: "any"` guarantees a tool call, so the output is always structured, while still letting the model pick the schema that matches the unknown document type. Why not the others: A allows text responses, which is exactly the 3% failure; C guarantees structure but applies the invoice schema to receipts and statements; D relies on a prompt instruction, which does not guarantee a tool call and leaves the plain-text failures in place.

bank.q: Your pipeline classifies incoming documents with a `doc_type` enum: invoice, receipt, contract, statement. Some documents are genuinely ambiguous, and new types such as customs declarations keep appearing; today the model forces them into the closest value, mislabeling about 5% of traffic. Analysts want to spot new types without weekly schema changes. How should you design the field?
o: Add an "unclear" enum value for ambiguous documents, plus an "other" value paired with a free-text detail field
Replace the enum with a free-text string so the model can describe any document type in whatever words it chooses
Keep the enum as is and instruct the model to always choose the closest value, so every document gets a known label
Keep the enum as is and reject any document that does not clearly match one of the four known types at intake
bank.w: An "unclear" value lets the model admit ambiguity instead of guessing, and "other" plus a detail string captures new types such as customs declarations without changing the schema, while known types keep a structured value. Why not the others: B loses the enum structure, producing inconsistent labels that are hard to aggregate; C is the current behavior that mislabels 5% of traffic; D rejects documents the pipeline could handle and hides the new types analysts want to see.

bank.q: Your invoice extraction pipeline asks Claude to return JSON. About 4% of responses come back as prose or as JSON wrapped in commentary, and the downstream parser rejects them, sending those invoices to a manual queue. One teammate proposes a stricter system prompt; another suggests a repair library. Which change MOST reliably guarantees schema-conformant output?
o: Add "respond with valid JSON only, no prose or commentary" to the system prompt, repeated at the end of the user message
Run every response through a JSON-repair library that strips commentary and fixes syntax before it reaches the parser
Define the extraction as a tool with a JSON input schema and read the structured data from the `tool_use` block
Raise `max_tokens` so long invoices are never truncated mid-object, which is what usually leaves the JSON unparseable
bank.w: Tool use with a JSON schema constrains the model to emit structured input that matches the schema, so stray prose and syntax errors are eliminated by construction rather than discouraged. Why not the others: A is a prompt request that is not enforced and leaves a residual failure rate; B patches symptoms after the fact and can silently produce wrong data; D addresses truncation, which is not the failure described: the problem is prose and commentary, not cut-off output.

bank.q: Your purchase order extraction schema marks `discount_code` as required. About 40% of orders genuinely have no discount, and audits find the model returning plausible codes such as "SPRING10" for them, which finance then tries to honor. The field must still be captured whenever a code is printed on the order. What is the correct schema design?
o: Keep `discount_code` required but default it to an empty string, so orders without a code still pass schema validation
Make `discount_code` optional and nullable, and instruct the model to return null when the order shows no code
Keep `discount_code` required and have the model emit a fixed placeholder such as "NONE" when no code is printed
Remove `discount_code` from the schema and have finance look up discounts manually in the ordering system instead
bank.w: A required field pressures the model to produce a value even when the source has none, which is what causes the fabricated codes. Making it nullable, with an instruction to return null when absent, lets the model report absence honestly while still capturing printed codes. Why not the others: A still forces a value, a fabricated empty string that conflates "no code" with an extraction gap; C is invented data that downstream systems may treat as a real code; D loses the field on the orders that do have one.

bank.q: Your extraction pipeline retries up to 5 times whenever validation fails. Cost analysis shows 18% of spend goes to documents that fail every retry; all of them are missing a required `tax_id`, which for these vendors appears only on a separate registration certificate that is never sent to the pipeline. What is the BEST change?
o: Raise the retry limit from 5 to 20 attempts, so the model has more chances to locate the `tax_id` in these documents
Keep `tax_id` strictly required and add a format pattern, forcing the model to produce a valid value on every pass
Retry these documents at a higher temperature, so that the model explores different readings of the document text
Detect when the value is absent from the source and route the document to review or accept null instead of retrying
bank.w: Retries with feedback fix format and structural errors, but they cannot recover information that is not in the source: the `tax_id` lives on a certificate the pipeline never receives. Detecting that case and routing it (human review or an accepted null) stops the wasted spend. Why not the others: A multiplies a cost that can never pay off; B pushes the model to fabricate an identifier; C changes sampling, not content, so it cannot surface data that is not there.

bank.q: Your invoice extraction uses `tool_use` with a strict JSON schema, and every output now passes validation. However, accounts payable found that about 2% of invoices have extracted line items that do not sum to the stated total, either from misread amounts or from errors on the invoice itself. These must be caught before payment. Which design BEST catches them?
o: Extract a `calculated_total` alongside the `stated_total` and set a `conflict_detected` flag when they differ
Mark the total field as required with a numeric type, so the schema forces the model to extract it correctly
Retry the extraction automatically until the extracted line items sum exactly to the stated invoice total
Switch from `tool_use` back to prose output, then parse the arithmetic out of the model's step-by-step text
bank.w: A strict schema eliminates syntax errors but not semantic ones: a well-formed invoice can still have totals that do not reconcile. Extracting both totals and flagging the conflict catches the mismatch whether the model misread an amount or the invoice itself is wrong, and sends it to review. Why not the others: B constrains type and presence, not arithmetic; C may push the model to alter values until they add up, hiding real invoice errors; D abandons the reliable structured path and reintroduces parsing failures.

bank.q: Your extraction occasionally returns a currency value that fails the downstream validator, such as "USD$" instead of the ISO code "USD", or "Euro" instead of "EUR". Each failure currently goes to a manual queue. You want the pipeline to self-correct automatically, but finance has capped the extra API spend per document. What is the soundest first approach?
o: Retry the identical request until an attempt passes validation, up to 50 times, since most failures are intermittent
Strip non-letter characters from the currency field in post-processing and pass the cleaned value on to validation
On failure, resend the document, the failed extraction and the specific validation error, capped at a few retries
Change the currency field to free text in the schema, so the validator no longer rejects nonstandard currency values
bank.w: Retry-with-error-feedback gives the model what it needs to fix the mistake: the source, its own output and the exact rule it broke, so a follow-up attempt usually corrects it, and a small cap keeps cost bounded as finance requires. Why not the others: A resends the same request with no new information, wasting spend on the same error; B is a brittle guess that fixes "USD$" but not "Euro"; D weakens the schema and pushes invalid values downstream.

bank.q: Your team generates technical-debt reports through the Message Batches API, which can take up to 24 hours and has no latency SLA. Stakeholders are promised each report within 30 hours of their request. Most batches finish in under two hours, so a teammate submits requests whenever convenient, sometimes a day after they arrive. How should you schedule submissions?
o: Keep submitting whenever convenient, since batches usually finish in under two hours and the promise rarely binds
Submit in fixed windows, such as every 4 hours, so that 24 hours of processing still fits inside the 30-hour promise
Move the reports to synchronous real-time calls, which removes the scheduling question at the cost of the discount
Submit when convenient, poll each batch every minute, and fall back to real-time calls if it runs over an hour
bank.w: Batch latency is not guaranteed, so scheduling must assume the 24-hour worst case: submitting in windows of a few hours leaves enough margin that even a full-length batch completes inside the 30-hour promise. Why not the others: A relies on typical speed, which carries no guarantee, and a late submission plus a slow batch breaks the promise; C gives up the 50% savings on a non-blocking job; D adds polling and fallback complexity and still pays real-time prices whenever batches are slow.

bank.q: You submit 100 contracts for extraction as one Message Batches request, each with a `custom_id` set to its contract number. The batch completes with 94 successes and 6 failures, all caused by documents exceeding the context limit. The 94 results are already validated and loaded. What is the MOST efficient way to handle the failures?
o: Resubmit the entire batch of 100 contracts so that all results come from the same run and share consistent settings
Discard the 6 failed contracts and accept 94% coverage, since the failures are a small share of the full batch
Move the whole workload to real-time calls so that failures like these surface immediately on future runs
Identify the 6 failures by `custom_id` and resubmit only those, chunking the oversized contracts into parts
bank.w: `custom_id` correlates each response with its request, so the failures can be identified and resubmitted on their own, and chunking fixes the cause (exceeding the context limit) instead of repeating it. Why not the others: A reprocesses 94 contracts that already succeeded and would fail the same 6 again; B silently drops data the pipeline is supposed to extract; C gives up the batch discount for the whole workload to solve a problem confined to six oversized documents.

bank.q: Two CI workflows call Claude synchronously: a pre-merge check that developers wait on before they can merge, and an overnight code-health report the team reads at 9 a.m. Your manager wants both moved to the Message Batches API for its 50% savings, noting that most batches finish in about an hour. Developers merge about 40 times a day. How should you evaluate this?
o: Move only the overnight report to the Batches API, and keep the blocking pre-merge check on synchronous calls
Move both workflows to the Batches API, and have the pipeline poll batch status until each check has completed
Keep both workflows synchronous, so the team avoids the added operational complexity of managing batch jobs
Move both to the Batches API, falling back to synchronous calls whenever a batch runs longer than 10 minutes
bank.w: The Batches API offers no latency SLA and can take up to 24 hours, which is fine for an overnight report but not for a check that blocks 40 merges a day; a typical one-hour completion is not a guarantee. Why not the others: B leaves a merge-blocking check exposed to unbounded latency; C forgoes the savings on a report nobody reads until morning; D adds fallback machinery, still makes developers wait, and often ends up paying real-time prices anyway.

bank.q: Your customer support agent resolves returns by calling `get_customer`, `lookup_order` and `process_refund` across several turns, reasoning over each tool result before choosing the next step. To cut costs, a teammate proposes running these conversations through the Message Batches API for its 50% discount. Why is this a poor fit?
o: The Batches API charges a premium for requests that include tool definitions, which cancels out the 50% discount
The Batches API cannot return structured JSON, so the agent's tool calls could not be parsed by the application
A batch request cannot run tools mid-request and continue with their results, and batches have no latency SLA
The Batches API accepts only one request per submission, so each customer turn would need its own separate batch
bank.w: The agent's workflow depends on executing a tool, feeding the result back and continuing to reason, which the Batches API does not support within a single request; batches can also take up to 24 hours with no latency SLA, unacceptable for a live customer. Why not the others: A is false, since batches are discounted, not surcharged; B is false, since batch requests can return the same structured output as synchronous ones; D is false, because a batch bundles many requests in one submission.

bank.q: Your CI reviewer analyzes each PR in a single pass. On a recent 20-file PR it gave detailed comments on the first few files, one-line remarks on the rest, and missed a bug where a renamed field in the API layer broke a consumer in the reporting module. Developers will not split their PRs. How should you restructure the review?
o: Require developers to break large PRs into submissions of 3 to 4 files each, enforced by a check that blocks larger PRs
Switch to a model with a larger context window, so that all 20 files fit comfortably into a single attentive pass
Run three identical full-PR passes and report only the issues that appear in at least two of the three passes
Review each file in its own pass for local issues, then run a separate integration pass focused on cross-file data flow
bank.w: Uneven depth is attention dilution, and the renamed-field bug is a cross-file data-flow issue. Per-file passes give every file the same focused analysis, while a dedicated integration pass looks specifically at how changes propagate across modules. Why not the others: A is ruled out by the constraint and shifts the burden to developers; B fits more text but does not fix attention quality across 20 files; C repeats the same diluted pass, and its consensus filter suppresses real bugs that are found only intermittently.

bank.q: Your pipeline has one Claude session write a data-migration module and then, in the same conversation, review it for bugs before merging. Over a month the review rated its own code clean 97% of the time, yet human reviewers later found bugs in 1 of every 5 modules. Most were edge cases the session's earlier reasoning had considered and dismissed. What is the MOST effective change?
o: Tell the generating session to "be more critical of your own work" and to list three possible bugs before approving
Have a separate Claude instance, without the generator's reasoning context, review the module before it is merged
Enable extended thinking on the generating session before it starts the review, so it deliberates longer on each change
Have the same session run its review twice with different wording, and merge the findings from both review passes
bank.w: The session retains the reasoning that led it to dismiss those edge cases, so it is unlikely to challenge its own decisions. An independent instance without that context reviews the code on its own terms and is better at spotting subtle issues. Why not the others: A asks for criticism but leaves the biasing context in place, and may produce filler findings; C adds deliberation inside the same biased context; D repeats the same session, reproducing its blind spot twice.

bank.q: Your support agent calls `lookup_order` several times per conversation, and each call returns 40+ fields such as warehouse codes and carrier metadata, though a return decision needs about 5 of them. By the third lookup, accuracy on return eligibility drops and the agent mixes up values between orders. The fix must keep the exact values a return depends on. Which change is MOST targeted?
o: Switch to a model with a larger context window and keep all 40+ fields per lookup, so nothing is ever unavailable
Summarize the whole conversation, order data included, into a short paragraph at the end of every turn
Trim each `lookup_order` result to the return-relevant fields before it is appended to the conversation context
Restart the conversation every few lookups, carrying over a brief note of what has been resolved so far
bank.w: The cause is tool output accumulating out of proportion to its relevance: 35+ unneeded fields per lookup crowd out what matters. Trimming each result to the return-relevant fields before it enters context removes the noise while keeping exact values intact. Why not the others: A gives the noise more room instead of removing it, so attention still dilutes; B is lossy summarization that risks blurring the exact values a return depends on; D discards history the agent still needs and adds friction for the customer.

bank.q: Your research coordinator concatenates the outputs of 12 subagents into one synthesis input of about 60K tokens. Reviewers find the final report reliably uses the first and last few results but omits findings from the middle, even when those directly answer the research question. Every finding must remain available to the synthesis agent. What BEST mitigates this?
o: Open the input with a key-findings summary and organize the detailed results under explicit section headers per subagent
Shuffle the order of the subagent results randomly on every run, so no single subagent is consistently buried in the middle
Drop the middle results before synthesis, since the model ignores them anyway and they only add token cost to each run
Concatenate the results in reverse chronological order, so the most recently completed subagents appear first
bank.w: This is the lost-in-the-middle effect: models process the start and end of long inputs reliably but miss mid-input content. Leading with a key-findings summary puts critical information in the strongest position, and explicit section headers help the model navigate the rest, while every finding stays available. Why not the others: B only moves the blind spot around from run to run; C throws away real findings, breaking the constraint; D reorders the input but still leaves a new set of results stuck in the middle.

bank.q: To save context in long support conversations, your agent condenses earlier turns into a short prose summary each turn. Customers now report it later quotes the wrong refund amount or order date; the summaries read like "a refund was discussed for a recent order". Context must still stay bounded in conversations that run 40+ turns. What is the BEST fix?
o: Summarize even more aggressively each turn, so there is less condensed text in which the agent could misstate a detail
Stop summarizing entirely and send the full raw transcript every turn, regardless of how long the conversation gets
Lower the sampling temperature so the agent reproduces numbers and dates from its summaries more accurately
Keep exact amounts, dates, order numbers and statuses in a persistent "case facts" block sent verbatim each turn
bank.w: Progressive summarization condenses numbers and dates into vague phrases, as the example summary shows. Extracting transactional facts into a persistent case facts block, kept outside the prose summary and included verbatim every turn, preserves them while the rest of the history stays summarized and bounded. Why not the others: A makes the loss worse; B defeats the requirement to keep context bounded in 40+ turn conversations; C cannot restore facts that the summary has already erased.

bank.q: A customer opens a chat with: "I don't want to deal with a bot. Connect me to a human." Their order history shows a routine late delivery, which the agent resolves in under two minutes 95% of the time, and the support team is short-staffed today. The agent has already started investigating. What should it do?
o: Finish the quick investigation first to save the human's time, and escalate only if it cannot resolve the late delivery itself
Honor the explicit request and escalate to a human immediately, without first attempting to investigate or resolve the issue
Explain how quickly it can fix late deliveries, and escalate only if the customer repeats the request a second time
Run sentiment analysis on the message and escalate only if the frustration score exceeds the configured threshold
bank.w: An explicit request for a human is an immediate escalation trigger and must be honored, however resolvable the issue looks and however busy the team is; overriding it to demonstrate capability damages trust. Why not the others: A does exactly what the customer asked the agent not to do; C makes the customer ask twice for something they already stated clearly; D substitutes an unreliable proxy (sentiment) for a signal that could not be clearer.

bank.q: A caller asks your support agent to update the shipping address on "my account, J. Smith." `get_customer` returns two distinct customers with that name, one active last week and one active two years ago, both with open orders. Once a shipment is relabeled, the change cannot easily be reversed. What is the BEST way for the agent to proceed?
o: Ask the customer for an additional identifier, such as their email or an order number, before changing anything
Select the account that was active last week, since a recently active customer is the most likely one to be calling
Select the first match returned by `get_customer`, then read the name back to the customer to confirm before editing
Escalate to a human agent immediately, since duplicate customer matches cannot be resolved inside the conversation
bank.w: Multiple matches call for asking the customer for an additional identifier: the customer knows definitively which account is theirs, and the hard-to-reverse change raises the cost of a wrong guess. Why not the others: B is heuristic selection, and recency says nothing about who is calling; C picks arbitrarily, and reading back a name that both accounts share confirms nothing; D over-escalates an ambiguity that one clarifying question resolves.

bank.q: Your support agent resolves only 60% of contacts on first contact, against an 85% target. Logs show it escalates clear-cut cases, such as standard warranty replacements with photos attached, while trying to handle ambiguous policy-exception requests itself. On those hard cases its stated reasoning sounds fully confident. What MOST effectively improves escalation calibration as a first step?
o: Have the agent emit a 1-10 confidence score each turn and route the case to a human automatically below a tuned threshold
Train a separate classifier on historical tickets to predict which contacts need escalation before the agent starts
Add sentiment analysis and escalate automatically whenever measured customer frustration exceeds a set threshold
Add explicit escalation criteria to the system prompt, with few-shot examples of when to escalate versus resolve
bank.w: The logs point to unclear decision boundaries: the agent cannot tell routine cases from policy exceptions. Explicit criteria with few-shot examples address that root cause directly and are the proportionate first step. Why not the others: A relies on self-reported confidence, which the logs show is already miscalibrated on the hard cases; B adds training and infrastructure before trying the simple prompt fix; C uses sentiment, which does not track case complexity, since a calm customer can still need a policy exception.

bank.q: A customer asks your support agent to waive a restocking fee because the item was a gift, and the buyer was never told about the fee. Your return policy defines the fee and when it applies, but says nothing about waivers in this situation. The customer is calm and has not asked for a human. What is the MOST appropriate action for the agent?
o: Deny the waiver politely, since nothing in the written policy authorizes the agent to remove a restocking fee
Grant the waiver as a goodwill gesture, since the fee is small and keeping the customer satisfied matters more
Escalate to a human, since the policy is silent on this request, even though the customer has not asked for one
Keep handling the request itself, and escalate only if the customer becomes upset or explicitly asks for a person
bank.w: A policy gap, where the policy is silent or ambiguous on the specific request, is a valid escalation trigger on its own, independent of any explicit request for a human. The agent should not invent policy in either direction. Why not the others: A treats silence as a prohibition, inventing a rule the policy does not state; B invents an exception the agent is not authorized to grant; D ties escalation to sentiment, which does not reflect that this is a policy question needing human judgment.

bank.q: Your research system is producing a market report with five subtopics. For one of them, regional regulation, the key sources were behind paywalls the search subagent could not access, so that section rests on two secondary blog posts. The other four sections are well sourced, and the report goes to executives who will act on it. How should the synthesis output BEST represent this?
o: Add coverage annotations showing which findings are well supported and where unavailable sources left gaps
Omit the regional regulation section entirely, so the report contains only material backed by strong sources
Fill out the thin section from the model's general knowledge so all five subtopics have comparable depth
Fail the whole report and retry later, since a decision document with an incomplete subtopic should not ship
bank.w: Coverage annotations implement graceful degradation with transparency: executives get the value of the four well-sourced sections and can see exactly where confidence is lower and why. Why not the others: B hides the gap, so readers may assume the topic was irrelevant rather than unresearched; C fabricates unattributed content presented as if it were researched; D discards a largely useful report over a single gap that can simply be disclosed.

bank.q: Your search subagent times out after 90 seconds on a broad query, having already gathered eight relevant sources. Today it retries silently and then reports only "search unavailable", so the coordinator either reruns everything or drops the subtopic. You are redesigning how this failure reaches the coordinator so it can recover intelligently. Which approach is BEST?
o: Keep retrying with exponential backoff inside the subagent, and return a generic "search unavailable" only after all retries fail
Return structured error context: the failure type, the query attempted, the partial results, and possible alternative approaches
Catch the timeout inside the subagent and return the eight sources as a normal successful result, without mentioning the timeout
Propagate the timeout to a top-level handler that aborts the whole research run, so no report rests on incomplete searches
bank.w: Structured error context gives the coordinator what it needs to decide: it can keep the eight sources, retry with a narrower query, or try another approach, instead of guessing from a bare status. Why not the others: A is the current behavior, and a generic status hides the partial results and the cause; C suppresses the failure, so the coordinator believes coverage is complete when it is not; D aborts a whole run over one recoverable failure and throws away all completed work.

bank.q: A developer has spent three hours in one Claude Code session mapping a legacy billing module. Early on, the agent identified the specific classes involved, such as `InvoiceBatcher` and `LedgerSync`; now its answers cite "typical patterns for billing systems" instead. The developer has many more questions and does not want to redo the discovery. Which practice MOST directly preserves the specific findings?
o: Lower the temperature for the rest of the session, so the agent recalls earlier specifics more consistently
Re-explore the relevant parts of the codebase from scratch for each new question, so every answer is freshly grounded
Ask the agent to keep all its answers shorter, so more of the earlier exploration still fits in the context window
Have the agent record key findings in a scratchpad file as it goes and consult that file for later questions
bank.w: Citing typical patterns instead of specific classes is a sign of context degradation in a long session. A scratchpad file persists key findings outside the context window, so later questions can draw on them even after earlier turns lose influence. Why not the others: A changes sampling, which does not bring back details that have degraded in context; B repeats the discovery the developer wants to avoid and burns more context; C saves little space and does nothing to preserve facts already found.

bank.q: Your multi-agent research job runs for about six hours across a coordinator and four subagents. Roughly once a week it crashes midway, from an API outage or a host restart, and the whole job restarts from zero, losing hours of completed work. You need the job to resume where it stopped, without redoing finished subagent tasks. Which design BEST enables this?
o: Run the whole job inside a single agent instead, eliminating coordination between agents as a source of crashes
Increase every agent's timeout and retry budget, so that each job has time to finish before a failure interrupts it
Have agents export structured state to a known location; on resume, the coordinator injects a manifest into prompts
Detect crashes automatically and re-run the whole pipeline immediately, so no one has to restart it by hand
bank.w: Crash recovery needs persisted state: structured exports from each agent, plus a manifest the coordinator loads on resume and injects into agent prompts, let finished work be reused instead of recomputed. Why not the others: A still crashes on outages and restarts, and gives up parallelism; B does nothing against outages or host restarts and recovers no state; D automates the restart but still repeats all the lost hours.

bank.q: Two hours into a Claude Code session investigating a flaky test suite, the context is filling with verbose discovery output: full file dumps, long `Grep` results and test logs. Responses are slowing and the agent is losing earlier specifics. The developer wants to reclaim context without abandoning the session's progress or setting anything new up. What is the MOST appropriate built-in step?
o: Run `/compact` to condense the session's context while keeping its essential state, then carry on
Exit and start a brand-new session from scratch, re-describing the problem so the context window begins empty
Raise `max_tokens` so the agent has more room to answer as the investigation's context keeps on growing
Lower the temperature so the agent's answers stay focused and stop drifting away from the earlier findings
bank.w: `/compact` is the built-in way to reduce context usage during a long investigation: it condenses the accumulated output while preserving essential state, so the session continues with its progress. Why not the others: B throws away the progress the developer wants to keep; C changes `max_tokens`, which limits output length and does nothing to relieve a full context window; D changes sampling, not how much context the session consumes.

bank.q: Your invoice and contract extraction pipeline reports 97% overall field accuracy on last month's 20,000 documents. Contracts are only 8% of the volume, and the payment-terms field is the one finance actually acts on. Leadership wants to cut human review by half starting next week. What should you verify FIRST before reducing review?
o: Nothing further: 97% is well above the 95% target, so start reducing review now and monitor complaints afterward
Whether the aggregate hides weak segments, measuring accuracy per document type and per field first
Whether raising the model's confidence threshold lifts overall accuracy above 98%, giving an extra safety margin
Whether a model with a larger context window would raise the aggregate accuracy figure further before the change
bank.w: Aggregate accuracy can mask poor performance on specific document types or fields: contracts are a small share of volume, so they could fail often while barely moving the 97%, and payment terms carry the real risk. Accuracy must be validated by segment before automating. Why not the others: A trusts a potentially misleading aggregate and finds problems only after harm is done; C and D chase a higher overall number without checking whether the segments that matter are safe.

bank.q: Your extraction pipeline auto-approves high-confidence results, about 70% of volume, and sends the rest to reviewers. A new supplier onboarding program will shift the document mix over the next quarter. Compliance wants ongoing evidence that the auto-approved set stays accurate, plus early warning of new error patterns. Which measurement approach BEST fits?
o: Keep reviewing only the extractions the model flags as low confidence, and track how often reviewers correct them
Re-run the full dataset weekly and compare total extracted values against the previous week's run to spot drift
Sample the auto-approved set until accuracy looks stable, then stop sampling and rely on the confidence scores
Regularly review a stratified random sample of auto-approved results to measure error rates and new patterns
bank.w: Only sampling the auto-approved set measures its real error rate, and stratifying (for example by supplier or document type) keeps the sample representative as the mix shifts, surfacing novel error patterns early. Why not the others: A never looks at high-confidence results, which is exactly where undetected errors would hide; B compares totals, which cannot reveal per-item errors; C stops measuring right before the document mix changes, abandoning the ongoing assurance compliance asked for.

bank.q: Your contract extraction pipeline processes 5,000 documents a day, but only two reviewers are available. Errors in fields like liability caps and termination dates are far costlier than errors in addresses, and the model sometimes extracts values that contradict each other across sections. How should you decide which extractions a human reviews to make the BEST use of reviewer time?
o: Have reviewers check a fixed random 10% of all extractions, regardless of field or document, for an unbiased sample
Review every extraction before it is released, adding temporary reviewers until the backlog is under control
Output field-level confidence, calibrate thresholds on labeled data, and route low-confidence or conflicting values
Review only the documents that took longest to process, since slow documents are the most likely to be complex
bank.w: Field-level confidence scores, with review thresholds calibrated against a labeled validation set, focus scarce reviewers on the extractions most likely to be wrong, and routing contradictory values catches the cross-section conflicts described. Why not the others: A ignores risk, spending most of the capacity on low-stakes fields; B exceeds the available capacity many times over; D uses processing time, a proxy unrelated to whether a field is correct.

bank.q: Your research system is preparing a report on electric vehicle adoption. Two credible sources, a national statistics agency and a respected industry association, report different market-share figures for the same year: 18% and 23%. Readers will use the figure in investment decisions. How should the synthesis BEST handle the conflict?
o: Keep both values, annotate the conflict, and attribute each figure to its own source
Report the higher figure, 23%, since industry associations often have more current market data
Report the average of the two figures, 20.5%, as a balanced estimate without further comment
Use the figure from whichever source the search subagent listed first, for consistency across runs
bank.w: Conflicting statistics from credible sources should be preserved with attribution and the conflict annotated, not resolved arbitrarily; readers making investment decisions need to see the disagreement and where each number comes from. Why not the others: B picks one value on an unverified assumption; C hides the disagreement and produces a number neither source reported; D chooses by list position, which is arbitrary.

bank.q: Your research system's synthesis step flagged two sources on remote-work adoption as "contradictory": one reports 22% and the other 35%. On review, the first figure comes from a 2021 survey and the second from a 2024 survey, and both are accurate. Subagent outputs today contain only the claim and the source URL. Which design change BEST prevents this kind of misreading?
o: Instruct the synthesis agent to always trust the more recent-sounding figure whenever two sources disagree
Drop every source older than the most recent one on the same topic before the synthesis step runs
Merge the two figures into a single averaged value, so the report presents one clear number to readers
Require subagents to include publication and data collection dates in their structured outputs
bank.w: The misreading came from missing metadata: without dates, a change over time looks like a contradiction. Requiring publication and collection dates in structured subagent outputs lets synthesis read the figures as a trend from 2021 to 2024. Why not the others: A guesses from how a figure sounds rather than from actual dates; B discards valid historical data that shows the trend; C averages values from different periods, which is meaningless.

bank.q: Your research system's final reports state facts correctly, but an audit found 30% of citations wrong or missing: subagents return prose summaries with sources listed at the end, and the synthesis agent loses track of which source supports which claim. Prompting it to "cite carefully" changed little. Which design BEST preserves attribution through synthesis?
o: Add a final instruction to the synthesis prompt asking it to double-check every citation before returning the report
Require subagents to output claim-source mappings (claim, excerpt, URL) that synthesis must preserve and merge
Have the synthesis agent re-derive citations at the end, matching each claim to the most plausible listed source
Drop inline citations and append a bibliography of all sources consulted, so no claim is ever mis-attributed
bank.w: Attribution is lost when claims and sources travel as unstructured prose. Structured claim-source mappings, with the claim, a supporting excerpt and the source, keep each link explicit, and synthesis must merge them rather than summarize them away. Why not the others: A is another prompt instruction, and the audit shows instructions changed little; C reconstructs links after they were lost, inviting fabricated citations; D gives up claim-level provenance entirely.

bank.q: Production metrics show your support agent averages 4+ API loops per resolution. Analysis shows that at the start of most conversations Claude needs both `get_customer` and `lookup_order`, yet requests them in separate sequential turns, adding a full round trip each time. The team wants fewer loops without changing the tool set. What is the MOST effective change?
o: Add speculative execution that also calls likely-needed tools alongside any requested tool and returns all results regardless
Increase `max_tokens` so Claude has more room to plan its next steps and naturally combines related tool requests on its own
Create a composite `get_customer_with_orders` tool that bundles the common lookup combination into one call for the agent
Instruct Claude in the prompt to request all the tools it needs in one turn, so every result returns before the next API call
bank.w: Claude can request several tools in a single response; prompting it to bundle the lookups it needs up front removes the extra round trip without touching the tool set, which is the team's constraint. Why not the others: A runs tools nobody asked for and floods the context with unrequested results; B changes the output budget, which is not what makes Claude split the requests; C changes the tool set, which the team wanted to avoid, and covers only one combination.

bank.q: You are implementing the agent loop for your support agent. After each Claude API call, the code must decide whether to run the requested tools and call Claude again, or stop and show the final answer to the customer. A teammate's prototype stops whenever the response contains any text, and it often ends before the refund tool runs. What should drive this decision?
o: The `stop_reason` field of the response: continue and run the tools when it is "tool_use", and stop when it is "end_turn"
Phrases in Claude's text such as "I'm done" or "Can I help with anything else?", which signal that the task is complete
A maximum iteration count, such as 10 calls, after which the loop stops regardless of whether Claude still needs tools
Whether the response contains assistant text, keeping the teammate's rule but also requiring at least one tool call first
bank.w: `stop_reason` is Claude's structured signal for loop control: "tool_use" means it is asking for tool results to continue, and "end_turn" means it has finished its response. A response can contain explanatory text and a tool request at the same time, which is why the prototype stops too early. Why not the others: B parses natural language, a documented anti-pattern; C uses an arbitrary cap as the primary control; D still keys on the presence of text, which does not mean the work is done.

bank.q: In your research system, the web search and document analysis subagents have both finished and returned their results to the coordinator: 22 web sources and 9 analyzed reports, with some overlap in claims. Stakeholders expect one integrated report with citations, and every inter-agent exchange must stay visible to the coordinator. What is the BEST next step?
o: Have each subagent send its results directly to the report generation subagent, bypassing the coordinator to save one hop
Have the document analysis subagent request the web search results and merge them internally with its own analyzed reports
Have the coordinator pass both sets of results to the synthesis subagent, which integrates them into one unified analysis
Have the coordinator concatenate the raw outputs of both subagents and return them to stakeholders as the final result
bank.w: In a hub-and-spoke design, the coordinator owns routing: it forwards both result sets to the synthesis subagent, which integrates overlapping claims into one analysis, and every exchange stays visible to the coordinator as required. Why not the others: A bypasses the coordinator and loses the required visibility; B makes a subagent talk to another subagent directly and assigns synthesis to the wrong role; D skips integration entirely, delivering raw, overlapping outputs instead of one report.

bank.q: You run your research system on "AI impact on creative industries". Every subagent completes successfully: search finds relevant articles, analysis summarizes them correctly, and synthesis is coherent. Yet the report covers only visual art and misses music, literature and film. The coordinator log shows the subtasks "AI in digital art", "AI in graphic design" and "AI in photography". What is the MOST likely root cause?
o: The synthesis subagent lacks instructions to detect coverage gaps, so it did not flag that music, literature and film were absent
The document analysis subagent's relevance criteria are too strict and filter out non-visual sources before they reach synthesis
The coordinator's decomposition is too narrow: its three subtasks are all visual art, so the other creative fields were never assigned
The web search subagent's queries are insufficient and should be broadened to cover more creative sectors in each of its searches
bank.w: The coordinator log is the decisive cue: all three subtasks it created are visual-art topics, so music, literature and film were never assigned, while each subagent executed its assignment correctly. The root cause is the narrow decomposition upstream. Why not the others: A might help notice the gap but did not cause it; B blames a filter for sources that were never in scope; D blames search, which correctly searched the visual-art subtasks it was given.

bank.q: In a design review of your research system, a colleague proposes letting the document analysis subagent send its results straight to the synthesis subagent, bypassing the coordinator to save a hop. Last quarter, two incidents came from a subagent receiving material it should not have seen, and another from a silent failure nobody noticed for days. What is the MOST important reason to keep the coordinator as the hub?
o: The coordinator observes every interaction, applies error handling uniformly, and controls exactly what information each subagent receives
The coordinator can batch requests to several subagents into fewer API calls, which lowers both total cost and end-to-end latency
Routing through the coordinator unlocks automatic retry logic for subagent calls, which direct agent-to-agent messages cannot support
Subagents keep isolated memory, so direct messages would need a complex serialization format that only the coordinator can produce
bank.w: A hub-and-spoke topology gives the coordinator visibility into every interaction, uniform error handling, and control over what context each subagent receives, which is exactly what the past incidents (leaked material and an unnoticed silent failure) lacked. Why not the others: B describes a cost and latency optimization that the hub pattern does not inherently provide and that would not have prevented the incidents; C is false, since retries can be implemented at any layer; D misreads context isolation: subagents receive context explicitly in their prompts, and passing results needs no special serialization.

bank.q: While researching a broad topic, you notice that the web search and document analysis subagents investigate the same subtopics in parallel, so their outputs overlap heavily. Token usage has nearly doubled without a matching gain in breadth or depth. The team wants to keep the parallel speedup and avoid adding new infrastructure. What is the MOST effective fix?
o: Let both subagents finish in parallel, then have the coordinator deduplicate overlapping results before passing them to synthesis
Have the coordinator explicitly partition the research space before delegating, giving each subagent distinct subtopics or source types
Add a shared-state store where subagents log their current focus area, so the others can steer away from it during execution
Switch to sequential execution, running document analysis after web search and passing it the search results as context
bank.w: The root cause is unclear task boundaries at delegation time. Partitioning the research space before delegating prevents the duplicated work from happening, keeps both subagents running in parallel, and needs nothing new. Why not the others: A cleans up after the tokens are already spent; C adds the infrastructure the team wants to avoid and depends on agents coordinating at runtime; D gives up the parallel speedup.

bank.q: Production logs show that in 12% of cases your support agent skips `get_customer` and calls `lookup_order` using only the name the customer typed, which has led to misidentified accounts and refunds issued on the wrong orders. The system prompt already asks for verification first. Identity must be verified before any order operation. What change MOST effectively fixes this?
o: Add few-shot examples showing the agent calling `get_customer` first, even when the customer volunteers order details up front
Add a routing classifier that analyzes each request and enables only the subset of tools appropriate for that request type
Add a programmatic precondition that blocks `lookup_order` and `process_refund` until `get_customer` returns a verified ID
Strengthen the system prompt to state that verification via `get_customer` is mandatory before any order operation
bank.w: Identity verification before financial operations requires a deterministic guarantee: a programmatic precondition makes it impossible to reach `lookup_order` or `process_refund` without a verified customer ID, whatever the model decides. The existing prompt and its 12% skip rate show guidance is not enough. Why not the others: A is prompt guidance and keeps a non-zero failure rate; B decides which tools are available, not the order they are called in; D is a stronger version of the instruction that is already failing.

bank.q: Production logs show your support agent misreading MCP tool outputs: Unix timestamps from `get_customer`, ISO 8601 dates from `lookup_order`, and numeric status codes (1=pending, 2=shipped). Some of these tools are third-party MCP servers you cannot modify, and new tools are added every quarter. Which approach to data normalization is MOST maintainable?
o: A `PostToolUse` hook that intercepts every tool output and applies the formatting transformations before the agent processes it
Modify the tools you control to return human-readable formats and write a separate wrapper for each of the third-party tools
A `normalize_data` tool that the agent is instructed to call after every data retrieval to transform the values it received
Detailed format documentation in the system prompt explaining each tool's data conventions, updated when a new tool is added
bank.w: A `PostToolUse` hook gives one central, deterministic point to normalize every tool result, including third-party MCP servers you cannot change, and new tools are covered by extending the same code. Why not the others: B spreads the logic across modified tools and per-tool wrappers that multiply as tools are added; C depends on the model remembering to call the tool every time, so normalization is probabilistic; D leaves interpretation to the model, the source of the current misreads.

bank.q: Your support agent resolves simple requests such as "refund for order #1234" in 3–4 tool calls with 91% success. For requests like "I was billed twice, my discount didn't apply, and I want to cancel", it averages 12+ calls with 54% success, investigating each issue in sequence and fetching the same customer data again for each one. What change MOST effectively improves complex requests?
o: Add verification checkpoints between stages, requiring the agent to record progress after each issue before moving to the next one
Combine `get_customer`, `lookup_order` and the billing tools into a single `investigate_issue` tool that the agent calls once per issue
Split the request into separate issues, investigate each in parallel with shared customer context, then synthesize one resolution
Add few-shot examples to the system prompt demonstrating ideal tool-call sequences for several multi-issue billing scenarios
bank.w: Both symptoms in the logs, sequential investigation and repeated customer lookups, are addressed by decomposition: each issue is investigated in parallel, the customer data is fetched once and shared, and one synthesized reply resolves everything. Why not the others: A adds bookkeeping but keeps the sequential, redundant pattern; B hides the investigation in one overloaded tool and still runs once per issue; D shows sequences by example without changing how the agent structures complex requests.

bank.q: Logs show requests like "analyze the uploaded quarterly report" being delegated to the web-search agent 45% of the time. Its tool `analyze_content` is described as "analyzes content and extracts key information", while the document analysis agent's `analyze_document` says "analyzes documents and extracts key information". You want to fix the root cause. What is the BEST change?
o: Add a pre-routing classifier that detects whether the user refers to uploaded files or web content before the coordinator delegates
Rename the web tool to `extract_web_results`, described as processing information retrieved from web search and URLs
Add few-shot examples to the coordinator prompt pairing uploaded reports with document analysis and web pages with web search
Expand only the document tool description with examples like "use for uploaded PDFs and spreadsheets", leaving the web tool as is
bank.w: The two names and descriptions are nearly identical, so the model cannot tell them apart. Renaming the web tool to `extract_web_results` and describing it in terms of web search and URLs removes the semantic overlap at its source, which is the root cause. Why not the others: A adds a component that works around ambiguous definitions instead of fixing them; C adds prompt weight while both tools still claim the same purpose; D clarifies one side only, so the generic `analyze_content` description still matches document requests.

bank.q: During pre-launch testing of your support agent, you see it call `get_customer` on 30% of order status questions such as "has my order shipped?", even though `lookup_order` is the right tool. The agent has only five tools, and nobody has looked at their definitions since the first prototype. What should you check FIRST?
o: Build a preprocessing classifier that detects order-related requests and routes them straight to `lookup_order`
Reduce the number of tools available to the agent, removing rarely used ones so the choice becomes simpler
Add few-shot examples to the system prompt that cover every order request pattern seen in testing so far
Check the tool descriptions to make sure they clearly differentiate the purpose and boundaries of each tool
bank.w: Tool descriptions are the primary input the model uses to choose a tool, and these have not been revisited since the prototype, so they are the first thing to check whenever a tool is consistently misselected. Why not the others: A adds infrastructure before checking the cheapest likely cause; B misses the issue, since five tools is already a manageable set; C tries to enumerate patterns instead of fixing the definitions the model relies on, and cannot cover every phrasing.

bank.q: Logs show that when customers write "account" (e.g., "check my account for an order I made yesterday"), the agent calls `get_customer` first 78% of the time; without it ("check an order I made yesterday"), it calls `lookup_order` first 93% of the time. Tool descriptions were recently reviewed and are clear. What is the MOST likely root cause?
o: Keyword-sensitive instructions in the system prompt that react to terms like "account" and steer the agent toward customer tools
Associations from the model's base training between "account" wording and customer operations that override tool descriptions
Insufficient training data on messages mixing account and order terms, which would require fine-tuning the model on such examples
Missing negative examples in the tool descriptions stating when not to use each tool, which lets one keyword cause confusion
bank.w: A sharp, systematic split driven by a single word, with clear tool descriptions, points to prompt-level instructions that react to "account" and steer the agent toward customer tools; system prompt wording is a known source of unintended tool associations. Why not the others: B is speculative and ignores the configuration you control, which is the usual source of keyword-driven patterns; C proposes fine-tuning for what is a prompt configuration issue; D targets the descriptions, which have already been reviewed and are clear.

bank.q: Production logs show the agent calling `get_customer` when users ask about orders (e.g., "check my order #12345") instead of `lookup_order`. Both tools have one-line descriptions ("Gets customer information" / "Gets order details") and accept similar-looking identifiers. The team wants a fix it can ship this week without adding infrastructure. What is the MOST effective first step?
o: Add a routing layer that analyzes user input before each turn and preselects the tool based on detected keywords and ID patterns
Merge both tools into a single `lookup_entity` that accepts any identifier and decides internally which backend to query
Add 5–8 few-shot examples to the system prompt showing order-related queries being routed to `lookup_order`
Expand each tool's description with input formats, example queries, edge cases, and when to use it versus the other tool
bank.w: The root cause is descriptions too thin for the model to tell two similar tools apart, and descriptions are the primary signal it uses for tool selection. Expanding them with input formats, example queries, and explicit boundaries is a low-effort, high-impact first step that needs no new infrastructure. Why not the others: A adds the infrastructure the team wants to avoid and replaces the model's understanding with keyword heuristics; B removes a useful distinction and hides the routing decision inside one overloaded tool; C can help, but it adds prompt weight to compensate for descriptions that remain uninformative, so it is not the best first step.

bank.q: You gave the document analysis agent a general-purpose `fetch_url` tool so it could download documents by URL. Logs now show it fetching search engine result pages to run its own ad hoc web searches, work that belongs to the web-search agent, and results have become inconsistent. You want the unwanted behavior to be impossible, not just discouraged. Which fix is MOST effective?
o: Replace `fetch_url` with a `load_document` tool that validates that each URL points to a supported document format
Remove `fetch_url` from the agent and route every URL fetch through the coordinator to the web-search agent instead
Add filtering that blocks `fetch_url` calls to known search engine domains while still allowing all other URLs
Add instructions to the agent's prompt that `fetch_url` may only be used to download documents, never to search
bank.w: Constraining the capability at the interface fixes the root cause: a `load_document` tool that validates document formats keeps the legitimate use and makes ad hoc searching impossible, following least privilege. Why not the others: B removes a capability the agent needs and adds coordinator round trips for every document; C is a denylist that misses any search engine or results page not on the list; D only discourages the behavior, which is not the guarantee required.

bank.q: Your synthesis agent often needs to verify claims while merging results. Each time, it returns to the coordinator, which calls the web-search agent and re-invokes synthesis, adding 2 to 3 loops per task and 40% latency. Analysis shows 85% of these are simple fact checks (dates, names, figures) and 15% need deeper research. Which approach BEST reduces overhead while preserving reliability?
o: Give the synthesis agent all of the web-search tools, so it can handle every verification itself without coordinator loops
Have synthesis collect all verification needs and return them to the coordinator as one batch at the end of the merge
Have the web-search agent cache extra context around each source during research, anticipating later verification needs
Give the synthesis agent a limited `verify_fact` tool for simple checks, and route complex ones through the coordinator
bank.w: A narrow `verify_fact` tool lets synthesis resolve the 85% of simple checks directly, removing most loops, while the 15% that need real research still go through the coordinator to the web-search agent. That is least privilege applied to a specific high-frequency need. Why not the others: A hands synthesis capabilities outside its role, which degrades tool selection and reliability; B still pays the round trip and leaves claims unverified while merging; C guesses at future needs, inflating context without guaranteeing the right facts are cached.

bank.q: Your team of six wants Claude Code to use a GitHub MCP server for searching PRs and checking CI status. Each developer has a personal GitHub access token. The lead wants identical tooling for everyone, defined once in version control, with no credentials committed and minimal setup for new hires. Which configuration is MOST effective?
o: Have each developer add the server in user scope with `claude mcp add --scope user`, following a wiki page
Build a wrapper MCP server that reads tokens from a `.env` file and proxies GitHub calls, and add it to `.mcp.json`
Add the server to the project `.mcp.json` with `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` substitution, and document the variable in the README
Configure the server in project scope with a placeholder token, and have developers override it in their local config
bank.w: A project `.mcp.json` is a single, version-controlled definition every developer gets on clone, and environment variable substitution lets each one supply their own token without committing it; documenting the variable keeps onboarding simple. Why not the others: A spreads the definition across six user configs that drift apart and is not in version control; B builds extra infrastructure for something substitution already handles; D relies on a placeholder that breaks for anyone who misses the override and duplicates the configuration.

bank.q: Three developers who have used Claude Code on your repo for months say it reliably follows the guidance "always include comprehensive error handling." A fourth developer who joined last week, on the same branch with up-to-date code, says Claude ignores it. Nobody remembers adding the guidance to any file in the repository. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
o: The guidance lives in the original developers' user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`; move it to the project `.claude/CLAUDE.md`
The new developer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` has conflicting instructions that override the project; delete that section
Claude Code learns per-user preferences over time, so the new developer must repeat the requirement until it sticks
Claude Code caches `CLAUDE.md` after first read, so the original developers see stale copies; clear everyone's cache
bank.w: Guidance in user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` applies only on each original developer's machine and is not shared through version control, which matches the fact that nobody added it to a repository file. Moving it to the project-level `.claude/CLAUDE.md` gives it to every current and future team member. Why not the others: B assumes a conflict, but the guidance is missing for the new developer, not overridden; C invents per-user learning that Claude Code does not do; D invents a caching behavior that would not explain why only some developers get the guidance.

bank.q: Your team's `CLAUDE.md` has passed 500 lines mixing TypeScript conventions, testing guidance, API patterns and deployment procedures. Two merge conflicts last week came from people editing unrelated sections at once, and developers struggle to find the part they own. You want focused topical modules using a mechanism Claude Code actually supports. Which approach fits?
o: Define a `.claude/config.yaml` that maps file patterns to specific sections of `CLAUDE.md`, so each area loads its part
Create separate Markdown files in `.claude/rules/`, one per topic, such as `testing.md` and `api-conventions.md`
Move instructions into README.md files in the relevant subdirectories, which Claude loads automatically as instructions
Create several `CLAUDE.md` files at different levels of the tree, each overriding its parent's instructions on a topic
bank.w: Claude Code supports a `.claude/rules/` directory of topic-focused Markdown files such as `testing.md` and `api-conventions.md`, which replaces a monolithic `CLAUDE.md` with modules that each owner can find and edit without conflicts. Why not the others: A relies on a `.claude/config.yaml` mechanism that does not exist; C assumes README files are loaded as instructions, which they are not; D organizes by directory rather than by topic, since nested files add context for a subtree instead of splitting topics.

bank.q: Your `CLAUDE.md` has grown to 400+ lines: coding standards, testing conventions, a detailed PR review checklist, deployment steps and database migration procedures. Claude must always follow the standards and testing conventions, but the review, deploy and migration guidance only matters during those tasks, which happen a few times a week. Which restructuring is MOST effective?
o: Move all guidance into separate skills organized by workflow type, leaving only a brief project description in `CLAUDE.md`
Keep everything in `CLAUDE.md` but use `@path` imports to split it into separately maintained files by category
Split it into `.claude/rules/` files with path globs so that each rule loads only when matching file types are edited
Keep the universal standards in `CLAUDE.md` and turn review, deploy and migration guidance into skills used on demand
bank.w: `CLAUDE.md` loads in every session, so the coding standards and testing conventions always apply, while skills are invoked on demand, so the review, deploy and migration guidance enters context only for those tasks. Why not the others: A makes the always-required standards optional; B improves maintenance, but imported files still load in every session, so nothing becomes task-specific; C scopes by file path, while these workflows are tied to tasks, not to the file types being edited.

bank.q: Your team's `/analyze-codebase` skill runs dependency scanning, test coverage counts and code quality metrics. After running it, developers report that Claude becomes sluggish and loses track of the task they were working on before the analysis. The team wants to keep the full analysis, with all three reports intact. Which change MOST effectively fixes this?
o: Add `context: fork` to the skill's frontmatter so the analysis runs in an isolated subagent context
Add `model: haiku` to the skill's frontmatter so the analysis runs on a faster and cheaper model
Split the skill into three smaller skills, one per report, so that each run produces less output
Instruct the skill to compress all results into a short summary before displaying them to the user
bank.w: `context: fork` runs the analysis in an isolated subagent context, so its large output does not fill the main session's context window and Claude keeps track of the original task, while the analysis stays complete. Why not the others: B changes speed and cost, not how much output lands in the main context; C still puts the same total output into the session, just in three steps; D trims the analysis, which conflicts with keeping all three reports intact.

bank.q: Your team's `/commit` skill lives in `.claude/skills/commit/SKILL.md`. One developer wants a different commit message format and two extra checks for their personal workflow, without editing the shared file or affecting teammates. Team docs and habits all say to run `/commit`, and the developer wants to keep typing that same command. What do you recommend?
o: Create a personal copy under `~/.claude/skills/` with a different name, such as `/my-commit`, and use that instead
Add conditional logic to the project skill's frontmatter that switches the format based on the developer's username
Create a personal version at `~/.claude/skills/commit/SKILL.md` with the same name, which takes precedence for them
Set `override: true` in the personal skill's frontmatter so it takes priority over the project version of `/commit`
bank.w: When skills share a name, a personal skill in `~/.claude/skills/` takes precedence over the project one, so `~/.claude/skills/commit/SKILL.md` changes `/commit` for that developer alone while the repository and teammates are untouched. Why not the others: A works but changes the command the developer wants to keep typing, and leaves two near-identical skills that can confuse automatic selection; B relies on a frontmatter capability that does not exist and edits the shared file; D invents an `override` field, since precedence comes from location.

bank.q: Including 2–3 full endpoint implementations as examples makes Claude's new API endpoints far more consistent. But the examples add about 3,000 tokens, and most work in `src/api/` is debugging and code review, where they only add noise. Developers want the examples loaded only when they are creating a new endpoint, without pasting them by hand. Which configuration is MOST effective?
o: Add the endpoint examples and pattern documentation to the project `CLAUDE.md` so they are available in every session
Have developers copy the relevant endpoint examples into the prompt manually each time they request a new endpoint
Add path-specific rules in `.claude/rules/` with the examples that activate whenever files in `src/api/` are edited
Create a skill that references the endpoint examples and pattern instructions, invoked on demand via a slash command
bank.w: A skill invoked on demand loads the examples only when a developer is creating a new endpoint, so debugging and review sessions in `src/api/` stay free of 3,000 tokens of noise and nobody has to paste anything. Why not the others: A loads the examples in every session, including unrelated work; B is the manual pasting the developers want to avoid; C scopes by directory, so the examples would still load during debugging and review, which also touch `src/api/`.

bank.q: Your `/migration` skill generates database migration files and takes the name via `$ARGUMENTS`. Production shows three problems: developers often run it without a name, producing badly named files; it sometimes uses schema details from unrelated earlier conversation; and once it ran destructive test cleanup because it had broad tool access. Which configuration fixes all three?
o: Switch to positional `$1` and `$2` parameters, reference schema files with `@` syntax, and add a description warning on cleanup
Add `argument-hint` to request the name, set `context: fork` to isolate execution, and limit `allowed-tools` to file writes
Split into `/migration-create` and `/migration-apply`, add instructions to ask for a missing name, and scope tools per skill
Add `SKILL.md` instructions to validate `$ARGUMENTS`, tell it to ignore earlier conversation, and list prohibited operations
bank.w: Each problem maps to a configuration feature: `argument-hint` prompts for the missing migration name, `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated context so earlier conversation cannot leak in, and `allowed-tools` limited to file writes blocks destructive commands. Why not the others: A changes parameter syntax without prompting for input and only warns about cleanup; C fixes tool scope but leaves context leakage and relies on instructions for the name; D relies entirely on prompt instructions, which are guidance rather than enforcement.

bank.q: Your team wants a `/review` slash command that runs its standard code review checklist. Right now three senior developers each keep slightly different copies on their own machines, and the checklists have drifted. The command must be identical for every developer who clones or updates the repository, and changes should go through pull requests. Where should you create the command file?
o: In `~/.claude/commands/` in each developer's home directory, synchronized by a shared script run during onboarding
In the project repository under `.claude/commands/`, so it is version-controlled and arrives with every clone or pull
In a `.claude/config.json` file in the repository, declared as one entry in an array of project-wide commands
In the root project `CLAUDE.md`, as a section that lists every step of the standard review checklist in order
bank.w: Commands in the project's `.claude/commands/` directory are version-controlled, so every developer gets the same `/review` after a clone or update, and changes go through pull requests, ending the drift between personal copies. Why not the others: A is user scope, which is how the copies drifted in the first place; C describes a configuration mechanism that does not exist for commands; D adds context to every session but does not define a slash command.

bank.q: Your team's `/explore-alternatives` skill brainstorms and compares implementation approaches before one is chosen. Developers report that afterwards Claude keeps referring to rejected approaches, and in one case reused a discarded data model during implementation. The exploration itself is valuable and should stay as thorough as it is. How should you configure the skill MOST effectively?
o: Use the `!` prefix in the skill to run the exploration logic as a bash subprocess, outside of the conversation
Add `context: fork` to the skill's frontmatter so the exploration runs in an isolated subagent context
Split it into `/explore-start` and `/explore-end` skills that mark when exploration context should be discarded
Move the skill from `.claude/skills/` to `~/.claude/skills/` so its exploration is personal to each developer
bank.w: `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated subagent context, so the brainstorming and rejected approaches never enter the main conversation and cannot leak into implementation, while the exploration stays as thorough as before. Why not the others: A runs shell commands, but the brainstorming is model reasoning, not a script; C cannot remove content that is already in the conversation; D changes who owns the skill, not where its context goes.

bank.q: Your monorepo mixes conventions: React components use hooks, API handlers use async/await with a specific error-handling wrapper, and database models follow the repository pattern. Test files sit next to the code they cover (e.g., `Button.test.tsx` beside `Button.tsx`), yet every test must follow the same conventions wherever it lives. What is the MOST reliable way to have Claude apply the right conventions automatically?
o: Put all conventions in the root `CLAUDE.md` under one heading per area and rely on Claude to infer which section applies
Create a skill in `.claude/skills/` for each code type, embedding that area's conventions in its `SKILL.md`
Place a separate `CLAUDE.md` in each subdirectory containing the conventions for the code in that directory
Create rule files in `.claude/rules/` whose YAML frontmatter uses glob patterns to apply conventions by file path
bank.w: Rule files in `.claude/rules/` with glob patterns in YAML frontmatter (e.g., `**/*.test.tsx`, `src/api/**/*.ts`) load conventions deterministically by file path, regardless of directory, which is what distributed test files need. Why not the others: A leaves the choice of section to inference, so it is neither automatic nor reliable; B makes conventions opt-in, since skills are invoked on demand rather than applied whenever a matching file is edited; C follows the directory tree, so it cannot express one test convention that spans every directory.

bank.q: You must add Slack as a notification channel.
