Email, SMS and push follow clear existing patterns, but Slack offers incoming webhooks (simple, one-way), bot tokens (delivery confirmation) or a Slack App (two-way events, needs workspace approval). The ticket just says "add Slack support", with no integration method or delivery-tracking requirement stated. How should you approach it?
o: Start in direct execution with incoming webhooks, since they match the existing one-way notification pattern
Use plan mode to explore the integration options and their implications, then recommend one before implementing
Start in direct execution by scaffolding a Slack channel class from existing patterns, deferring the method choice
Start in direct execution with a bot token, so delivery confirmation is available if the team needs it later on
bank.w: Slack offers several valid integration methods with different architectural implications, and the ticket leaves the choice open, so plan mode is the right fit: explore the options, weigh the trade-offs and agree on one before implementing. Why not the others: A and D each commit to a method on an assumption the ticket does not support; C writes code before the decision that shapes it, risking rework once the integration method is chosen.

bank.q: You've been asked to split your team's monolithic billing application into microservices. The work touches dozens of files and requires decisions about service boundaries, shared modules and data ownership, and two senior engineers already disagree on where the boundaries should be. A mistake here is expensive to undo. Which approach should you choose?
o: Use plan mode to explore the codebase, map dependencies and design the approach before any changes are made
Start in direct execution and switch to plan mode only if unexpected complexity appears during implementation
Start in direct execution with small incremental changes, letting the implementation reveal natural boundaries
Use direct execution with detailed upfront instructions that specify the structure of every planned service
bank.w: Plan mode suits large architectural restructuring: Claude explores the codebase and maps dependencies safely, so boundary decisions are made on evidence before expensive changes land across many files. Why not the others: B ignores complexity that is already known up front; C lets boundaries emerge from code changes, which is costly to undo if they turn out wrong; D assumes the service structure is settled when the engineers still disagree on it.

bank.q: You're adding error-handling wrappers around external API calls in a 120-file codebase, in three phases: discover call sites, design the approach together with Claude, then implement it consistently. In phase 1, Claude's listing of hundreds of call sites fills the context window before discovery finishes. The design decisions must stay in context for implementation. What is MOST effective?
o: Use an Explore subagent for phase 1 to isolate verbose discovery and return a summary, then do phases 2–3 in the main session
Do all phases in the main conversation, running `/compact` periodically to reduce context usage as you work through files
Switch to headless mode with `--continue`, passing explicit context summaries between batch calls to keep continuity
Define the pattern in `CLAUDE.md`, then process files in batches across separate sessions that share only that memory file
bank.w: An Explore subagent keeps the verbose discovery in its own context and returns a concise summary, leaving the main context for the collaborative design and the implementation, where the agreed decisions must stay available. Why not the others: B lets discovery fill the context and then compresses it, which can lose design details; C fragments the work into batch calls held together by hand-written summaries; D splits implementation across sessions, losing the collaborative design context.

bank.q: You asked Claude Code to write a function that turns third-party API responses into your internal normalized format. After two iterations, nested fields still land in the wrong place and timestamps come out in the wrong format. Your prose requirements are complete, but Claude interprets them differently each time. Which approach is MOST effective for the next iteration?
o: Write a JSON schema for the expected output and validate Claude's output against it after each iteration
Provide 2–3 concrete input and output examples showing the expected result for representative responses
Rewrite the requirements more precisely, with exact field mappings, nesting rules and timestamp format strings
Ask Claude to explain its current understanding of the requirements to find where interpretations diverge
bank.w: Concrete input and output examples show the exact expected result, including nesting and timestamp format, which removes the ambiguity of prose that Claude keeps reading differently. Why not the others: A detects mismatches after each iteration but never shows Claude how inputs should map to outputs; C is still prose, which is the root cause of the divergence; D diagnoses the misunderstanding without giving Claude an unambiguous target.

bank.q: Your CI runs Claude Code with `--print` and `CLAUDE.md` for project context, and developers find the reviews substantive. But findings arrive as narrative paragraphs that someone copies into PR comments by hand. The team wants a script to post each finding as an inline comment, which needs file path, line number, severity and suggested fix in a reliable format. Which approach is MOST effective?
o: Add an "Output Format for Review" section to `CLAUDE.md` with examples of structured findings to follow
Use `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` to enforce structured findings, then post them via the GitHub API
Require in the review prompt that each finding follow a template such as `[FILE:path] [LINE:n] [SEVERITY:level]`
Keep the narrative review, then add a second Claude step that summarizes the findings into a structured JSON list
bank.w: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` enforces structured output at the CLI level, so every finding arrives with file path, line number, severity and suggested fix in a form the script can parse and post as inline comments. Why not the others: A is guidance through examples, which improves consistency but does not enforce the format; C is a prompt-level template that can still drift and needs fragile parsing; D adds a second model call whose output still lacks an enforced schema.

bank.q: Your automated review suggests test cases for each PR. On a PR that adds course completion tracking, Claude suggested 10 tests, and developers found that 6 duplicated scenarios already covered in `completion.test.ts`. Duplicates like this appear on most PRs, and developers have started ignoring the suggestions. What change MOST effectively reduces duplicate suggestions?
o: Include the existing test file in context so Claude can see which scenarios the suite already covers
Reduce the requested suggestions from 10 to 5, assuming Claude ranks the most valuable cases first
Instruct Claude to focus only on edge cases and error conditions, since success paths are usually tested
Add post-processing that drops suggestions whose descriptions share keywords with existing test names
bank.w: Claude can only avoid suggesting covered scenarios if it can see what the suite already tests, so including the existing test file fixes the root cause and lets it propose genuinely new cases. Why not the others: B cuts volume without telling Claude what is covered, so duplicates can remain; C guesses at coverage and can skip success paths that are actually missing; D filters on keyword overlap, which misses reworded duplicates and can drop valid suggestions.

bank.q: An automated review left 12 findings on a PR. The developer pushed commits addressing most of them, and the re-run produced 8 findings, 5 of which repeat earlier comments on code the new commits already fixed. Developers are starting to dismiss the bot's comments unread. The review must stay thorough across the whole PR. What is the MOST effective way to eliminate the redundant feedback?
o: Run the review only when the PR is opened and again in its final pre-merge state, skipping intermediate commits
Add a post-processing filter that drops findings matching earlier ones by file path and issue description
Restrict the review to files changed in the most recent push, excluding files touched by earlier commits
Include the previous review findings in context and instruct Claude to report only new or still-unresolved issues
bank.w: With prior findings in context, Claude can compare them against the new commits and report only what is new or still unresolved, removing the redundant comments while still reviewing the whole PR. Why not the others: A delays feedback during the iterations where it is most useful; B would also drop findings that are still unresolved, since a match on path and description does not mean the issue was fixed; C narrows coverage, which breaks the requirement to keep the review thorough across the PR.

bank.q: Your nightly security pipeline runs `claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues"`, and every run stalls until the CI runner kills it hours later. Logs show Claude Code waiting for interactive input. Another engineer suggests redirecting stdin from `/dev/null`. You want the documented way to run Claude Code in an automated pipeline. What is the correct approach?
o: Add a `--batch` flag: `claude --batch "Analyze this pull request for security issues"`
Add the `-p` flag: `claude -p "Analyze this pull request for security issues"`
Redirect stdin from `/dev/null`: `claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues" < /dev/null`
Set the environment variable `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` in the job before running the `claude` command
bank.w: The `-p` (`--print`) flag is the documented way to run Claude Code non-interactively: it processes the prompt, prints the result to stdout and exits without waiting for input, which suits automated pipelines. Why not the others: A uses a `--batch` flag that Claude Code does not have; C is the suggested workaround, which masks the hang instead of selecting non-interactive mode; D relies on an environment variable that is not a Claude Code feature.

bank.q: Your CI reviewer checks comments and docstrings with the instruction "check that comments are accurate and up to date." Developers report it flags harmless TODO markers and short descriptive comments, yet it missed a docstring claiming a function retries three times when the retry loop was removed last sprint. What change addresses the root cause of this inconsistent analysis?
o: Include `git blame` data in the prompt so Claude can identify comments that were written before recent code changes
Add few-shot examples of misleading comments so the model recognizes similar patterns elsewhere in the codebase
Filter out TODO, FIXME and short descriptive comments before analysis, so the reviewer sees less noise per file
Specify explicit criteria: flag a comment only when the behavior it describes contradicts what the code actually does
bank.w: "Accurate and up to date" does not define what a problem is, so the model guesses: it flags harmless patterns and misses the docstring describing retries the code no longer performs. An explicit criterion, a contradiction between claimed and actual behavior, fixes both errors at their source. Why not the others: A uses age as a proxy, but old comments can be correct and new ones wrong; B can help but leaves the vague instruction in place; C hides some noise without defining what to flag, so the misses remain.

bank.q: Your CI review's false-positive rates differ by category: security and correctness 8%, performance 18%, naming and style 52%, documentation 48%. Surveys show developers now dismiss findings unread because "half are wrong," including the accurate security ones. Improving the weak categories' prompts will take several weeks. Which approach BEST restores trust while the system improves?
o: Temporarily disable the style, naming and documentation categories, keeping the precise ones while prompts improve
Keep every category enabled but show a confidence score on each finding, so developers can choose what to investigate
Keep every category enabled and add few-shot examples to each, improving their accuracy gradually over the weeks
Apply one uniform strictness reduction across all categories to bring the overall false-positive rate down to target
bank.w: Noisy categories erode trust in the accurate ones, and the prompt fixes are weeks away. Disabling the 48-52% categories now stops the erosion while security and correctness keep delivering value, and leaves room to improve and re-enable the others. Why not the others: B pushes triage onto developers using self-reported confidence, which is poorly calibrated; C keeps the noise in front of developers for weeks while trust keeps falling; D also suppresses findings in the 8% categories that are already precise.

bank.q: Your CI reviewer finds real issues, but developers call the feedback not actionable: findings say "complex ticket routing logic" or "potential null pointer" without saying what to change. You added "always include a concrete fix suggestion with the exact location," yet output still alternates between detailed and vague. Which prompting technique MOST reliably produces consistently actionable feedback?
o: Refine the instructions further with explicit requirements for each part of the format: location, issue, severity, fix
Expand the context to include more of the surrounding codebase, so the model has enough information to propose fixes
Split the work into two prompts, one that identifies issues and a second that generates a concrete fix for each issue
Add 3–4 few-shot examples showing the exact format: the identified issue, its location in code, and a concrete fix
bank.w: When explicit instructions already produce variable results, few-shot examples are the most effective way to obtain consistent, actionable output: a few concrete findings with a location and a specific fix give the model a pattern to reproduce. Why not the others: A adds more of the instructions that have already proven insufficient; B assumes missing information, but the model finds real issues and the problem is how it reports them; C adds a second call and pipeline complexity without addressing format consistency.

bank.q: Your support agent picks the right tools 94% of the time for single-issue messages like "refund order #1234." When a message combines issues, such as a refund for #1234 plus an address change for #5678, accuracy falls to 58%: it handles only one issue or swaps order numbers between tools. The team wants a fix without new pipeline components. What is MOST effective?
o: Add a preprocessing model call that splits multi-issue messages into separate requests, handles each, and merges results
Combine the related refund, shipping and order tools into fewer general-purpose tools that accept several actions at once
Add few-shot examples showing the reasoning and tool sequence for multi-issue messages, keeping each issue's parameters apart
Add response validation that detects incomplete answers and automatically reprompts the agent to resolve any missed issues
bank.w: The agent already handles single issues well; what it lacks is a pattern for decomposing a combined message and keeping each issue's parameters separate. Few-shot examples demonstrating that reasoning and tool sequence target exactly this gap with no new components. Why not the others: A adds the pipeline component the team wants to avoid; B makes tool selection less precise and does nothing about mixed-up parameters; D detects misses after the fact and does not prevent parameters being swapped between orders.

bank.q: Logs show your support agent calling `get_customer` when `lookup_order` fits better, mostly on vague messages like "I need help with my recent purchase." Clear requests such as "where is order #4417?" are routed correctly 99% of the time. Tool descriptions were already expanded last sprint, and the team now wants to add few-shot examples to the system prompt. Which approach is MOST effective?
o: Add explicit "use when" and "don't use when" guidance to each tool description, covering the ambiguous purchase requests
Add examples grouped by tool, with all the `get_customer` scenarios first followed by all the `lookup_order` scenarios
Add 4–6 examples aimed at the ambiguous requests, each explaining why one tool was chosen over the plausible alternative
Add 10–15 examples of clear, typical requests for each tool, demonstrating the correct choice in the most common cases
bank.w: Errors concentrate on ambiguous requests, while clear ones already work. A few examples targeted at those edge cases, with the rationale for choosing one tool over the other, teach the comparative decision the model is getting wrong. Why not the others: A is not a few-shot approach and repeats description work already done; B organizes examples by tool rather than by the decision that is failing; D spends prompt space on cases that already succeed 99% of the time and says nothing about ambiguity.

bank.q: Your CI code review is iterative: Claude analyzes the changed file, then calls a `read_file` tool your application defines to fetch imports, base classes and tests, and continues its analysis with the results before giving feedback. Reviews average six tool calls each. To cut API cost, you are evaluating the Message Batches API. What is the primary technical limitation for this workflow?
o: Batch processing has no correlation IDs, so the application cannot map each review's output back to its originating PR
A batch request cannot pause to execute a tool and return its result so that Claude can continue the same analysis
The Batches API does not accept tool definitions in request parameters, so `read_file` could not be offered to Claude
The batch latency of up to 24 hours is too slow for PR feedback, though the workflow would otherwise run unchanged
bank.w: Each review needs several rounds of tool call, tool execution and continued reasoning. A batch request is processed asynchronously with no point at which your application can run `read_file` and hand the result back, so the iterative workflow cannot run inside it. Why not the others: A is false, since `custom_id` correlates requests and responses; C is false, since the problem is executing tools mid-request, not declaring them; D treats latency as the main issue, but the workflow would not function in a batch at all.

bank.q: Your CI runs three Claude analyses: style checks on every PR that block merging until they finish, a weekly security audit of the whole codebase, and nightly test generation for recently changed modules. Finance wants the 50% discount of the Message Batches API, whose processing can take up to 24 hours, without slowing developers down. Which assignment is MOST appropriate?
o: Batches API for all three tasks to maximize the 50% savings, with the pipeline polling until each batch completes
Synchronous calls for the PR style checks; the Batches API for the weekly security audit and the nightly test generation
Synchronous calls for all three tasks for consistent response times, relying on prompt caching to reduce the cost
Synchronous calls for the PR style checks and nightly test generation; the Batches API only for the weekly audit
bank.w: PR style checks block developers, so they need synchronous calls; the weekly audit and the nightly generation are scheduled, latency-tolerant jobs that fit inside a 24-hour batch window, capturing the discount on both. Why not the others: A puts a merge-blocking check behind a window of up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee; C gives up the 50% discount on two workloads that do not need fast responses; D keeps nightly test generation on synchronous calls even though nothing waits on it overnight.

bank.q: Your CI pipeline has two Claude review modes: a pre-merge hook that blocks the merge until it finishes, and a "deep analysis" that runs overnight, polls for completion and posts detailed suggestions to the PR by morning. You want to cut API cost with the Message Batches API, which offers 50% savings but requires polling and can take up to 24 hours. Which mode should use batch processing?
o: Only the pre-merge hook, since it runs most often and therefore accounts for the largest share of total API spend
Only the deep analysis, since it already runs overnight, tolerates delay, and polls for its results before posting
Both modes, with the pre-merge hook polling for its batch results just as the overnight deep analysis already does
Neither mode, since the polling that the Batches API requires adds too much complexity to the existing CI pipeline
bank.w: The deep analysis already fits the batch model: it runs overnight, nobody waits on it, and it already polls before posting, so it captures the 50% savings with almost no change. Why not the others: A puts a merge-blocking hook behind a window of up to 24 hours with no latency SLA; C does the same for the hook, leaving developers unable to merge for hours; D gives up the savings on a job whose design already matches batch processing.

bank.q: To reduce API cost, your manager proposes moving two synchronous CI workflows to the Message Batches API: a blocking pre-merge check that must finish before a developer can merge, and a technical-debt report generated overnight and reviewed the next morning. A teammate worries batch results may come back in a different order than submitted. How should you evaluate the proposal?
o: Move both to batch processing, with a fallback to synchronous calls whenever a batch takes longer than expected
Move both workflows to batch processing, with status polling to confirm completion before results are used
Use batch processing only for the overnight technical-debt report; keep synchronous calls for pre-merge checks
Keep synchronous calls for both workflows, since batch results can return out of order and break the pipeline
bank.w: The Batches API can take up to 24 hours with no latency SLA: acceptable for a report reviewed the next morning, unacceptable for a check developers are waiting on. Matching each workflow to its latency requirement captures the savings where they cost nothing. Why not the others: A adds fallback complexity and still leaves developers waiting until the fallback triggers; B gives the blocking check unbounded latency; D overstates the ordering risk, since `custom_id` maps each result to its request regardless of order.

bank.q: Your team uses Claude Code to generate refactoring suggestions. Non-obvious problems, such as a performance optimization that breaks an empty-list edge case, are caught only when a teammate reviews the PR. The generation transcripts show Claude considered these exact cases and concluded its approach was correct. Which approach directly addresses the root cause of this self-check limitation?
o: Run a second, independent Claude Code instance to review the changes without access to the generator's reasoning
Enable extended thinking for the generation stage, so Claude deliberates more thoroughly before making suggestions
Add self-review instructions to the generation prompt, asking Claude to critique its suggestions before finishing
Include the full test files and documentation in the generation context, so Claude understands expected behavior
bank.w: The transcripts show the cases were considered and rationalized, so the problem is not missing deliberation but a reviewer anchored to its own reasoning. An independent instance without that context, like a human peer reviewer, judges the code fresh and catches what the author talked itself out of. Why not the others: B adds more reasoning inside the same anchored context; C asks the author to critique itself while keeping the bias; D adds information, but the model already considered these cases and still reached the wrong conclusion.

bank.q: A PR changes 14 files in your inventory tracking module. The single-pass CI review gives detailed feedback on some files and shallow comments on others, misses an obvious off-by-one bug, and flags a locking pattern in one file while approving identical code in another. The team wants consistent depth plus coverage of how stock counts flow between files. How should you restructure the review?
o: Run three independent full-PR review passes and flag only the issues that appear in at least two of the three runs
Review each file in its own focused pass for local issues, then run a separate integration pass on cross-file data flow
Require developers to split large PRs into smaller submissions of 3–4 files each before the automated review runs
Switch to a larger model with a bigger context window so it can give enough attention to all 14 files in one pass
bank.w: Uneven depth, missed obvious bugs and contradictory verdicts are symptoms of attention dilution in a single pass. Per-file passes give every file the same focused analysis, and a separate integration pass covers the cross-file stock-count flow the team cares about. Why not the others: A repeats the diluted pass three times, and its consensus filter can drop real bugs found only once; C shifts the burden to developers instead of fixing the review; D adds context capacity, not consistent attention across files.

bank.q: On complex billing disputes and multi-order returns, your support agent's satisfaction scores are 15% below simple cases even when the resolution is correct. Transcript reviews show the explanations are inconsistent: some omit the relevant policy, others the refund timeline or next steps, and the missing piece differs from case to case. You must improve quality without adding human review. What is MOST effective?
o: Add a self-critique stage in which the agent checks its draft for completeness: policy context, timelines, next steps
Add a closing step where the agent asks "Does this fully resolve your issue?" so customers can request missing details
Route complex cases from Haiku to Sonnet based on a defined complexity metric, so harder cases get a stronger model
Add few-shot examples of complete explanations for the five most common complex case types to the system prompt
bank.w: The gaps vary case by case, so a fixed set of examples cannot anticipate them; a self-critique stage (evaluator-optimizer) checks each draft against concrete completeness criteria and fills whatever is missing before the customer sees it, with no human involved. Why not the others: B pushes the burden onto the customer after an incomplete answer has already been delivered; C changes the model, but the solutions are already correct and nothing targets completeness; D covers five common types, while the missing pieces vary from case to case.

bank.q: Monitoring shows inconsistent synthesis quality. With aggregated inputs of about 75K tokens, the synthesis agent reliably cites the first 15K tokens (web search snippets) and the last 10K (document analysis conclusions), but often misses critical findings in the middle 50K, even when they directly answer the research question. Which restructuring of the aggregated input is MOST effective?
o: Summarize all subagent outputs to under 20K tokens before aggregation, keeping the input within a reliably processed range
Stream results incrementally: process all web search results to completion first, then add the document analysis results
Put a key-findings summary at the start of the input and organize detailed results under explicit section headings
Rotate which subagent's results appear first across research tasks, so both sources get equal top positioning over time
bank.w: The pattern is the lost-in-the-middle effect. A key-findings summary at the start places critical information where the model attends most reliably, and explicit section headings help it navigate mid-input content. Why not the others: A compresses aggressively and risks discarding the very details that answer the question; B still leaves a long middle region once both sets are combined; D only shifts which subagent's findings get buried, varying quality instead of fixing it.

bank.q: In testing, your web search subagent returns 85K tokens, mostly raw page content, and the document analysis subagent returns 70K, including its full reasoning. The combined 155K tokens go to a synthesis agent that performs best under 50K. Synthesis needs facts, quotes and sources, not page text or reasoning traces. Which solution is MOST effective?
o: Change upstream subagents to return structured data (key facts, quotes, relevance scores) instead of verbose content
Add an intermediate summarization agent that condenses all findings into a shorter digest before they reach synthesis
Have the synthesis agent process findings in sequential batches, maintaining a running state between successive calls
Store all findings in a vector database and give the synthesis agent search tools to query them during its work
bank.w: The volume comes from content synthesis does not need. Having upstream subagents return structured data fixes the root cause at the source, cutting tokens while keeping the essential facts, quotes and sources. Why not the others: B adds an extra agent, cost and latency, and its lossy summary can drop details; C works around the volume instead of removing it and adds state-management complexity; D adds infrastructure and makes synthesis depend on retrieving the right chunks.

bank.q: Your support agent summarizes history once context reaches 70% of the window. Logs show customers referencing specifics like "the 15% discount I mentioned" and the agent replying with wrong values: those details came up 20+ turns earlier and were condensed into "promotional pricing was discussed". Such values must be reliably available on every turn. What fix is MOST effective?
o: Raise the summarization threshold from 70% to 85% of the window, so conversations get more room before summarizing
Store the full history externally and retrieve from it whenever the agent detects phrases such as "as I mentioned"
Extract amounts, dates and order numbers into a persistent "case facts" block in every prompt, outside the summary
Revise the summarization prompt to preserve every number, percentage, date and customer-stated expectation verbatim
bank.w: Summarization inherently loses precise details. Extracting transactional facts into a structured case facts block, kept outside the summarized history and sent with every prompt, makes them available on every turn no matter how much history has been condensed. Why not the others: A only delays the loss; B depends on detecting reference phrases, which customers do not always use, and adds retrieval infrastructure; D still relies on the summarizer complying, and repeated re-summarization keeps degrading what it keeps.

bank.q: Your support agent's first-contact resolution is 55%, against an 80% target. Logs show it escalates simple cases, such as standard replacements for damaged goods with photo proof, while handling complex policy-exception requests on its own. The team wants a proportionate fix that addresses the cause without adding new infrastructure. Which approach is MOST effective?
o: Have the agent self-rate its confidence from 1 to 10 before each response, routing to a human below a set threshold
Deploy a separate classifier trained on historical tickets to predict which requests need escalation upfront
Add explicit escalation criteria to the system prompt, with few-shot examples of when to escalate versus resolve
Add sentiment analysis to measure customer frustration and escalate automatically past a negative threshold
bank.w: The root cause is unclear decision boundaries between simple and complex cases. Explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples teach the agent where the line is, the proportionate first fix with no new infrastructure. Why not the others: A relies on self-rated confidence, an unreliable proxy, since the agent is already confident on the cases it mishandles; B adds a trained model and infrastructure the team wants to avoid; D measures frustration, which does not track whether a case needs a policy exception.

bank.q: Your support agent has called `get_customer` and `lookup_order` and has all available system data, yet still faces uncertainty in four open conversations. Your guidelines say it should resolve whatever falls within its scope and policies, and reserve `escalate_to_human` for cases that need human judgment. Which situation MOST justifies calling `escalate_to_human`?
o: A customer wants to cancel an order that shipped yesterday and arrives tomorrow, and admits they may change their mind
Tracking shows a disputed order delivered and signed for three days ago, and the customer will likely be upset to hear it
A customer asks for a competitor price match; policy covers price drops on your own site within 14 days but not competitors
A customer's single message mixes a billing question about last month's invoice with a request to return a product
bank.w: Competitor price matching is a genuine policy gap: the rules cover price drops on your own site but say nothing about competitors, so the agent must not invent policy and should escalate for human judgment. Why not the others: A is a standard cancellation within the agent's scope, and a possible change of mind is no reason to escalate; B is resolvable by presenting the tracking evidence tactfully, since an upset reaction is not a policy gap; D is two routine requests the agent can decompose and handle in sequence.

bank.q: Your `get_customer` tool returns every match when searching by name. When there are several, Claude currently picks the customer with the most recent order, and production data shows this selects the wrong account 15% of the time on ambiguous matches, sometimes exposing another customer's order details. How should you address this MOST reliably?
o: Add a confidence score to each match, acting autonomously above 85% confidence and asking for clarification below it
Have Claude ask for another identifier, such as email, phone or order number, before any customer-specific action
Change `get_customer` to return only the single most likely match from a ranking algorithm, removing the ambiguity
Add few-shot examples to the prompt showing correct reasoning and tool sequencing for handling ambiguous matches
bank.w: The customer has definitive knowledge of their own identity, so asking for an additional identifier resolves the ambiguity rather than guessing at it; one extra turn is a small price for eliminating a 15% wrong-account rate with privacy consequences. Why not the others: A still acts on a guess above the threshold, and the scores may be miscalibrated; C hides the ambiguity inside the tool, so wrong picks continue silently; D improves reasoning, but no reasoning can tell same-name customers apart without more information.

bank.q: Your document analysis subagent often fails on PDFs: some have corrupted sections that throw parsing exceptions, some are password-protected, and the parser occasionally hangs on large files. Today every exception ends the subagent with a bare error, and the coordinator must decide whether to retry, skip, or fail the task, so it spends much of its time on routine recovery. Which change is MOST effective?
o: Add a dedicated error-handling agent that watches a shared failure queue and sends restart commands directly to subagents
Always return partial results with a success status, putting error details in metadata so the coordinator never intervenes
Have the coordinator pre-validate every document and reject any that might fail before it is sent to the subagent
Recover locally from transient failures and escalate only what the subagent cannot resolve, with attempted steps and partial results
bank.w: Errors should be handled at the lowest level able to resolve them: local recovery (e.g., retrying a hang with a timeout) removes routine work from the coordinator, while unrecoverable cases such as a password-protected file still reach it with the context it needs to decide. Why not the others: A adds another agent and a second control path instead of fixing where errors are handled; B is silent error suppression, since failures reported as successes mislead every downstream step; C cannot reliably predict corruption or hangs and would reject documents that might have parsed fine.

bank.q: Your web search subagent returns results for only 3 of 5 requested source categories: competitor sites and industry reports succeed, while news archives and social feeds time out. The document analysis subagent processes every document successfully. The synthesis subagent must now summarize these mixed inputs, and readers need to know how far to trust it. Which error-propagation strategy is MOST effective?
o: Continue synthesis with the successful sources and produce the summary without mentioning which data was unavailable
Have the synthesis subagent return an error to the coordinator, triggering a full retry or failure over incomplete data
Have the synthesis subagent ask the coordinator to retry the timed-out sources with a longer timeout before it starts
Produce the summary with coverage annotations marking well-supported conclusions and gaps from missing sources
bank.w: Coverage annotations implement graceful degradation with transparency: they keep the value of the completed work while propagating uncertainty, so readers know which conclusions are solid and where news and social coverage is missing. Why not the others: A hides the gaps, so readers overtrust the summary; B throws away good results from three categories and the document analysis over a partial failure; C stalls synthesis on retries that may time out again, and retry decisions belong to the coordinator rather than the synthesis step.

bank.q: Midway through a 40-document research task, your document analysis subagent hits a corrupted PDF it cannot parse. The coordinator has options the subagent lacks: it can look for another copy of the report, skip it, or tell the user that a key source is missing. You are designing how the system handles this failure. Which approach is MOST effective?
o: Return an error with context (the file, the failure, what was tried) so the coordinator can decide how to proceed
Silently skip the corrupted document and continue processing the remaining files so the workflow is never interrupted
Retry parsing the same file three times with exponential backoff inside the subagent before reporting a failure
Throw an exception that terminates the entire research workflow, so no report is produced from an incomplete set
bank.w: Returning an error with context lets the coordinator, which has the broader options, make an informed decision: find another copy, skip the file, or notify the user, while the failure stays visible. Why not the others: B suppresses the failure, so the report may silently lack a key source; C retries a deterministic failure, since a corrupted file will not parse on the third attempt either; D aborts 39 documents' worth of work over one bad file.

bank.q: While researching a complex regulatory topic, your web search subagent times out after collecting part of what it needed. The coordinator could retry with a narrower query, switch to another source, or continue with what was found, but today it receives only a bare exception. You are redesigning how this failure is reported. Which error-propagation approach BEST enables intelligent recovery?
o: Return structured error context: failure type, query executed, any partial results, and alternative approaches
Catch the timeout inside the subagent and return an empty result set marked as successful, so the workflow keeps moving
Retry with exponential backoff inside the subagent, and return a generic "search unavailable" status once retries run out
Propagate the timeout exception to the top-level handler, terminating the research workflow until the issue is fixed
bank.w: Structured error context gives the coordinator exactly what its recovery options need: the failure type and executed query support a narrower retry, partial results allow continuing, and suggested alternatives point to other sources. Why not the others: B suppresses the failure and reports false success, discarding the partial results; C hides the cause and the partial results behind a generic status; D aborts the whole workflow over a single recoverable timeout.

bank.q: During one research task, your web search subagent queries three source categories: academic databases return 15 relevant papers, industry reports return "0 results", and patent databases return "Connection timeout". The coordinator must decide what to retry and what to trust, and every unnecessary retry costs several minutes. Which error-propagation approach enables the BEST recovery decisions?
o: Aggregate outcomes into a single coverage metric such as "67% source coverage", with detailed logs available on demand
Report both the timeout and the "0 results" outcome as failures, each requiring an intervention from the coordinator
Retry both unsuccessful categories inside the subagent, the empty one included, and report only what still fails afterward
Report the timeout as an access failure needing a retry decision, and "0 results" as a valid result of a successful query
bank.w: A timeout and "0 results" mean different things: the first is an access failure whose outcome is unknown, the second a successful query that found nothing, which is itself informative. Distinguishing them lets the coordinator retry only the patent databases and accept the empty industry result. Why not the others: A collapses both into one number that hides which source needs action; B treats a valid empty result as a failure, prompting a wasted retry; C also retries the empty category for nothing and hides from the coordinator what happened.

bank.q: Your CI code review averages 15 findings per pull request, and developers report a 40% false-positive rate. The bottleneck is investigation time: developers must click into each finding to read Claude's rationale before fixing or dismissing it. `CLAUDE.md` already lists acceptable patterns, and stakeholders rejected any approach that filters findings before developers see them. What change BEST reduces investigation time?
o: Have Claude include its rationale and a confidence estimate directly in each finding, visible without opening it
Add a post-processor that suppresses findings matching historical false-positive signatures before they are posted
Categorize findings as "blocking issues" or "suggestions", each with different review requirements for developers
Configure Claude to post only high-confidence findings, filtering out uncertain flags before developers see them
bank.w: Putting the rationale and a confidence estimate inline lets developers triage each finding at a glance instead of opening it, which attacks investigation time directly while every finding stays visible, as stakeholders require. Why not the others: B filters findings before developers see them, which was rejected; C changes how findings are prioritized, but developers still have to open each one to judge it; D is the same filtering stakeholders ruled out.

bank.q: Your document analysis subagent finds that two credible sources disagree on a key metric: a government report states 40% growth, an industry analysis states 12%. The discrepancy could materially change the research conclusions. The coordinator sees all subagent outputs and the research brief; the analysis subagent sees only its assigned documents. How should the analysis subagent MOST effectively handle this?
o: Apply credibility heuristics to pick the likelier figure, finish the analysis with it, and add a footnote on the discrepancy
Include both figures in the output without marking them as conflicting, and let synthesis choose using broader context
Stop the analysis and escalate to the coordinator at once, asking which source is more authoritative before continuing
Finish the analysis with both figures, annotate the conflict with source attribution, and let the coordinator reconcile it
bank.w: Preserving both values with an explicit, attributed conflict keeps the analysis complete and unblocked, and hands reconciliation to the coordinator, which has the broader context the subagent lacks. Why not the others: A resolves the conflict with limited context and buries the disagreement in a footnote; B passes the conflict on unmarked, so synthesis may never notice it; C blocks the analysis on a decision that can be made after the work is done.

bank.q: You are implementing the agent's core loop. Which control flow correctly determines when to keep executing tools and when to present the final response?
o: Continue looping until the assistant's text contains a phrase like "I have resolved the issue", then stop
Inspect `stop_reason` on each response: while it is "tool_use", execute the requested tools and return results for the next iteration; when it is "end_turn", present the final response
Run exactly five iterations, since support cases rarely need more tool calls than that
Stop as soon as any response contains text content, since text indicates completion
bank.w: The agentic loop keys off `stop_reason`: "tool_use" means the model has requested tools and expects their results back; "end_turn" means it has finished reasoning and produced its answer. That signal is the designed termination mechanism. Why not the others: A parses natural language for a completion signal, a documented anti-pattern; C makes an arbitrary iteration cap the primary stopping mechanism; D fails because responses can contain both text and `tool_use` blocks mid-task.

bank.q: The agent calls `lookup_order` and your code executes it successfully. How does the model actually receive the order data so it can reason about the next action?
o: The MCP server pushes the result directly into the model's memory
The model re-reads the tool's description, which now includes the result
Nothing is required: the API executes tools and incorporates results automatically
Your code appends a tool result block (referencing the tool call's ID) to the conversation history and sends the updated messages back to Claude in the next request
bank.w: Tool execution is the harness's job: the loop appends the tool result to the conversation and re-invokes the model. That growing history is the only channel through which the model sees what tools returned. Why not the others: A and C describe automatic mechanisms that do not exist (the API does not execute your tools); B confuses static tool definitions with runtime results.

bank.q: Company policy caps autonomous refunds at $500; larger refunds must go to a human. In testing, prompt instructions alone still let an occasional $650 refund through. What is the correct enforcement design?
o: Implement a hook that intercepts outgoing `process_refund` calls, blocks any amount above $500, and redirects the agent to the `escalate_to_human` workflow
Move the $500 limit to the top of the system prompt and repeat it in every user turn
Lower the model temperature so it follows the policy more consistently
Add the limit to the `process_refund` tool description so the model reads it during selection
bank.w: Business rules with financial consequences need deterministic guarantees. A tool-call interception hook enforces the threshold in code (the violating call can never execute), while prompt-based approaches remain probabilistic. Why not the others: B and D improve the odds but retain a non-zero failure rate, which the scenario shows is unacceptable here; C misapplies a sampling parameter to a compliance problem.

bank.q: A customer writes one message containing three concerns: a refund for a damaged item, a shipping address change, and a missing loyalty credit. How should the agent handle this?
o: Resolve only the refund, since it was mentioned first, and wait for the customer to raise the others again
Escalate immediately, since multi-issue messages always exceed agent capability
Decompose the message into three distinct items, investigate each (in parallel where possible) using the shared customer context, then synthesize one unified resolution covering all three
Ask the customer to resend each issue as a separate message
bank.w: Multi-concern decomposition is the designed pattern: split the request into distinct items, investigate each against shared context, and respond once with a complete resolution, protecting first-contact resolution. Why not the others: A and D silently drop or bounce concerns the customer already stated, directly harming FCR; B escalates work that is well within capability.

bank.q: The agent must escalate a complex billing dispute mid-process. The human agents receiving escalations do not have access to the conversation transcript. What should the escalation include?
o: Only the customer's name, so the human can start fresh without bias
A structured handoff summary: customer ID, the root cause analysis so far, relevant amounts and order numbers, and the agent's recommended action
A sentiment score describing how upset the customer is
The raw JSON of every tool result gathered during the session
bank.w: Structured handoff protocols exist precisely because the receiving human lacks the transcript: the summary transfers the case state (identity, findings, figures, and a recommendation) so the customer never has to start over. Why not the others: A discards completed investigation and forces repetition; C conveys mood, not case state; D transfers unprocessed noise and leaves the analysis to be redone.

bank.q: Yesterday you ran a long investigation into a memory leak in a session you named `leak-hunt`. Today you want to continue exactly where that investigation left off. What do you run?
o: `claude --continue-all`, which reopens every recent session
`claude --resume leak-hunt`, resuming the named session with its context
`claude -p "continue the leak investigation"`
A new session, pasting yesterday's terminal scrollback as the first message
bank.w: Named session resumption is the mechanism for continuing specific prior work: `--resume <session-name>` restores that conversation's context so the investigation picks up where it stopped. Why not the others: A is not a real flag; C starts a fresh non-interactive run with no memory of yesterday; D approximates resumption badly, since unstructured scrollback is a poor substitute for the session's actual context.

bank.q: You have completed a thorough analysis of a module and now want to compare two competing refactoring strategies, developing each independently from that same analysis baseline without the explorations contaminating each other. Which capability fits?
o: Run both strategies sequentially in the same session, asking Claude to forget the first before starting the second
Open two brand-new sessions and redo the module analysis in each
Use `/compact` between the two strategies
Use `fork_session` to create independent branches from the shared analysis baseline, exploring one strategy per branch
bank.w: `fork_session` exists for divergent exploration: both branches inherit the completed analysis, then evolve independently, giving a clean comparison without re-paying the analysis cost or cross-contaminating approaches. Why not the others: A is impossible, since context cannot be selectively forgotten on request; B pays for the expensive baseline twice; C compresses context within one session, it does not branch it.

bank.q: You want to resume last week's refactoring session, but since then the team has merged substantial changes across the files it analyzed, so most of its tool results now describe code that no longer exists. What is the reliable approach?
o: Start a new session seeded with a structured summary of the prior conclusions, since stale tool results make resumption unreliable: the model will reason from outdated file contents
Resume the session as-is; Claude automatically detects file changes
Resume the session and increase `max_tokens` to accommodate the confusion
Never resume any session; always start from zero exploration
bank.w: The resumption tradeoff: resume when prior context is mostly valid; start fresh with an injected summary when tool results have gone stale. Heavily changed files put this squarely in the second case: keep the conclusions, discard the outdated evidence. Why not the others: B assumes an automatic re-verification that does not happen, so stale results sit in context as if true; C spends tokens on a correctness problem; D throws away a valid technique: for minor changes, resuming and informing the session which files changed works well.

bank.q: Your coordinator's system prompt tells it to delegate research to subagents, but at runtime it never spawns any; it attempts all the research itself. Its configuration restricts it to research-planning tools. What is the most likely cause?
o: The coordinator model tier is too small to understand delegation
Subagents must be started manually before the coordinator runs
The system prompt needs the word "delegate" in capital letters
The coordinator's `allowedTools` does not include "Task"; the `Task` tool is the mechanism for spawning subagents, so without it no delegation can occur
bank.w: Subagent spawning happens through the `Task` tool. A coordinator whose `allowedTools` omits "Task" has no mechanism to delegate, no matter how clearly its prompt describes the intention: capability configuration trumps instruction. Why not the others: A and C look for the failure in comprehension or emphasis when the tool inventory makes delegation impossible; B describes a startup model that does not exist, since subagents are spawned on demand.

bank.q: The web search subagent gathers excellent findings, but the synthesis subagent's reports are generic and reference none of them. The coordinator invokes synthesis with the prompt "Synthesize the research findings." What is wrong?
o: The synthesis agent's model needs extended thinking enabled
Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history; the coordinator must include the actual findings (search results, analysis outputs) directly in the synthesis subagent's prompt
The synthesis agent needs web search tools to gather its own findings
The prompt needs the word "please"
bank.w: Subagent context isolation is the rule: each subagent sees only what its prompt contains. "The research findings" refers to material the synthesis agent has never seen, so the coordinator must pass the findings explicitly. Why not the others: A adds reasoning capacity over an empty input; C duplicates the search agent's role instead of fixing the handoff; D is not the missing ingredient: data is.

bank.q: The coordinator currently invokes the web search subagent, waits for completion, then invokes the document analysis subagent, doubling research latency even though the two tasks are independent. How do you run them in parallel?
o: Have the coordinator emit both `Task` tool calls in a single response, which spawns the subagents in parallel
Ask each subagent to work faster in its system prompt
Run two copies of the entire system and merge the databases
Parallelism is impossible; subagents must always run sequentially
bank.w: Parallel spawning is achieved by emitting multiple `Task` tool calls in one coordinator response rather than across separate turns; independent workstreams then execute concurrently. Why not the others: B changes nothing about scheduling; C is massive infrastructure duplication for a one-line orchestration fix; D is false, since parallel `Task` calls are a documented pattern.

bank.q: Your coordinator gives subagents rigid step-by-step procedures ("run these exact five queries in this order"). Subagents fail whenever a topic doesn't fit the script. How should coordinator prompts be designed instead?
o: Make the procedures longer, covering more contingencies explicitly
Remove all instructions and let subagents infer their tasks
Specify research goals and quality criteria (what a complete answer looks like) and let the subagent adapt its approach to what it discovers
Have subagents ask the human operator whenever the script fails
bank.w: Goal-and-criteria prompts preserve subagent adaptability: the coordinator defines success, the subagent chooses the path, which is why the agent (not a fixed script) is there at all. Why not the others: A is an arms race against topic variety that scripts always lose; B removes the goal along with the script; D reintroduces a human into a loop designed to run autonomously.

bank.q: Completed reports are coherent but shallow on some subtopics. You want the system to notice and repair its own coverage gaps before finalizing. Which orchestration pattern achieves this?
o: Lower the bar: accept the first synthesis as final to control costs

An iterative refinement loop: the coordinator evaluates synthesis output for gaps, re-delegates to search and analysis subagents with targeted queries, and re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient
Ask the report generation agent to pad thin sections with general knowledge
Always run every subagent exactly twice regardless of output quality
bank.w: Iterative refinement closes the quality loop: evaluate coverage, dispatch targeted follow-up research where gaps exist, re-synthesize, repeating until the report meets criteria rather than hoping the first pass suffices. Why not the others: A ships the known defect; C fills gaps with uncited generalities, the opposite of a cited research product; D doubles cost blindly with no gap detection to aim the second pass.

bank.q: The task is open-ended: "add comprehensive tests to this legacy codebase." Nobody knows yet where the risk concentrates or what depends on what. Which decomposition approach fits?
o: First map the codebase structure, identify high-impact areas, then create a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies and surprises are discovered
Write tests file-by-file in directory order until done
Generate all tests in a single maximal request
Test only the code modified in the last month
bank.w: Open-ended tasks call for adaptive decomposition: understand the terrain, prioritize by impact, and let the plan evolve with what each step reveals, the opposite of a fixed pipeline chosen before anything is known. Why not the others: B spends effort by directory-listing order rather than risk; C asks one pass to do what requires discovery; D uses recency as a proxy for importance, while legacy risk often lives in old, untouched code.

bank.q: You are choosing decomposition strategies for two workflows: a code review that always checks the same five aspects, and a production-incident investigation whose next step depends on what each finding reveals. Which pairing is right?
o: Dynamic decomposition for both, since flexibility is always better
Prompt chaining for both, since fixed steps are easier to test

Prompt chaining (a fixed sequence of focused passes) for the predictable five-aspect review; dynamic adaptive decomposition for the investigation, where intermediate findings determine the next subtask
Dynamic decomposition for the review; prompt chaining for the investigation
bank.w: The selection rule: fixed sequential pipelines for predictable multi-aspect work, adaptive decomposition where the path emerges from intermediate findings. Each workflow gets the structure its uncertainty profile demands. Why not the others: A pays adaptivity overhead on a task with no uncertainty; B forces an investigation to follow steps written before the evidence existed; D assigns each strategy to the workflow that defeats it.

bank.q: You are writing `AgentDefinition` configurations for the productivity system's subagents. Which statement about subagents is accurate?
o: Subagents automatically inherit the parent agent's full conversation history
Subagents can be spawned without the `Task` tool if the prompt describes them clearly
Subagents do not share memory between invocations; whatever context a subagent needs must be provided explicitly in its prompt
Subagent tool restrictions are advisory and not enforced at runtime
bank.w: Subagents are isolated: no inherited history, no memory across invocations, so context passing is always explicit. Another accurate statement is that each subagent's `AgentDefinition` carries its own description, system prompt, and tool restrictions for its role. Why not the others: A and B invert the isolation and spawning models (context never flows automatically, and `Task` is the spawning mechanism); D is false, since tool restrictions are configuration, not suggestion.

bank.q: When `process_refund` fails for any reason, it currently returns the string "Operation failed." The agent responds by retrying policy-blocked refunds and giving up on temporary outages, the opposite of correct. What is the fix?
o: Instruct the agent in the system prompt to always retry exactly twice
Remove failure responses entirely so the agent never sees errors
Have the agent apologize to the customer whenever any error occurs
Return structured error metadata: an `errorCategory` (transient / validation / business / permission), an `isRetryable` boolean, and a human-readable description the agent can act on
bank.w: Uniform error strings deny the agent the information recovery decisions require. Structured metadata (category, retryability, description) lets it retry transient failures, explain business refusals, and stop wasting attempts on non-retryable errors. Why not the others: A hard-codes one recovery strategy for error types that need different ones; B removes the signal instead of enriching it; C treats communication as a substitute for correct recovery logic.

bank.q: A refund request violates the returns window policy. The tool rejects it. Which error response enables the agent to handle this correctly with the customer?
o: `errorCategory`: "business", `retriable: false`, plus a customer-friendly explanation of the policy, so the agent explains the refusal rather than retrying it
`errorCategory`: "transient" so the agent retries later, when the policy might differ
An empty result marked as success, to keep the conversation positive
A stack trace, so the agent has maximum detail
bank.w: Policy violations are business errors: non-retryable by definition, and best paired with an explanation the agent can relay. The `retriable: false` flag prevents wasted attempts; the friendly description powers the customer conversation. Why not the others: B mislabels a deterministic refusal as temporary, guaranteeing futile retries; C is silent error suppression, an anti-pattern that turns failure into misinformation; D exposes internals the agent cannot use and should not repeat.

bank.q: The agent frequently confuses `get_customer` and `lookup_order`; both currently carry one-line descriptions. Which description change most directly fixes the misrouting?
o: Make both descriptions shorter so there is less to confuse
Prefix both descriptions with "IMPORTANT:" for emphasis
Add boundary language differentiating the two, e.g., "use `lookup_order` when an order number is present; use `get_customer` to verify identity before account operations"
Rely on the tool names alone, since names are what models read
bank.w: Descriptions are the primary selection mechanism, and explicit boundary language resolves precisely the overlap causing the misrouting. A complementary practice is documenting each tool's expected input formats and adding example queries it should handle. Why not the others: A removes information from tools that already have too little; B adds emphasis without discrimination; D is false: names help, but descriptions carry the selection signal.

bank.q: Every subagent currently receives the full 18-tool catalog. Logs show the synthesis agent attempting web searches and the search agent trying document parsing, with frequent wrong-tool selections everywhere. What is the correct redesign?
o: Add a nineteenth tool that tells the agents which tool to use
Alphabetize the tool list so selection is easier
Write longer system prompts warning each agent about the tools it should ignore
Scope each subagent's tool set to its role (a handful of relevant tools each), since large tool inventories degrade selection reliability and out-of-role tools invite misuse
bank.w: Tool distribution is an architectural control: agents choose more reliably among 4–5 role-relevant tools than among 18, and tools outside an agent's specialization are misused precisely because they are available. Why not the others: A adds selection complexity to solve selection complexity; B changes ordering, not decision difficulty; C asks prompts to fight an inventory problem configuration should fix.

bank.q: Subagents burn many tool calls just discovering what data exists (listing available document collections, probing for issue summaries, checking what schemas are present) before real work begins. Which MCP capability reduces this?
o: Expose content catalogs (document hierarchies, issue summaries, schema listings) as MCP resources, giving agents visibility into available data without exploratory tool calls
Increase the tool-call budget so exploration is affordable
Hard-code the current data inventory into every system prompt
Remove discovery capability so agents work blind
bank.w: MCP resources exist for exactly this: exposing catalogs of available content so agents start informed. Discovery becomes a lookup instead of a spelunking expedition of exploratory calls. Why not the others: B pays for the inefficiency rather than removing it; C goes stale the moment the data changes; D trades wasted calls for ignorance.

bank.q: The agent must (a) locate every file matching the test naming convention anywhere in the repo, and (b) find every place the string "PaymentDeclinedError" appears in code. Which ONE of these tool selections is correct?
o: `Glob` with a pattern like `**/*.test.tsx` for the test files, since file-path pattern matching is `Glob`'s job
`Grep` with a filename pattern to find the test files
`Glob` for "PaymentDeclinedError" across file contents
`Bash` running `cat` on every file, piping through manual inspection
bank.w: The division of labor is clean: `Glob` matches file paths against patterns (names, extensions, directories); `Grep` searches file contents for patterns (identifiers, error strings, imports). The other correct selection for this task, not listed here, is `Grep` for "PaymentDeclinedError". Why not the others: B and C swap the tools into each other's territory; D abandons both purpose-built tools for a brute-force pipeline that floods context.

bank.q: The agent attempts an `Edit` on a legacy file and fails: the anchor text it targeted appears in six places, so the unique-match requirement cannot be satisfied. What is the standard fallback?
o: Delete five of the six occurrences so the match becomes unique
Retry the same `Edit` repeatedly until it succeeds
Switch to `Bash` and modify the file with `sed`
Use `Read` to load the full file, then `Write` the complete modified content, the reliable path when `Edit` cannot find unique anchor text
bank.w: `Edit` depends on unique text matching; when a file's repetitive structure defeats that, `Read` + `Write` performs the modification reliably on the whole file. It is the documented fallback for exactly this failure. Why not the others: A mutilates code to satisfy the tool; B retries a deterministic failure, since the sixfold match will not resolve itself; C swaps a controlled file operation for fragile stream editing.

bank.q: Asked how the billing module works, the agent Reads dozens of files upfront and exhausts its context before answering. What is the correct exploration strategy for building codebase understanding?
o: `Read` files in alphabetical order and stop at the context limit
Work incrementally: `Grep` to find entry points (key functions, imports, error strings), then `Read` selectively to follow imports and trace flows from those anchors
Ask the developer to explain the module instead
`Read` only the README and reason from documentation
bank.w: Incremental exploration is the pattern: search first to find where the relevant code lives, then read narrowly along the traced paths. Context is spent on the files that matter rather than on everything alphabetically prior to them. Why not the others: A spends the budget by filename accident; C outsources the agent's job to its user; D trusts documentation to describe code accurately, which in a legacy system is a famous last assumption.

bank.q: The team shares a GitHub MCP server that needs an auth token, and you also run a personal, experimental MCP server you don't want to impose on anyone. How should these be configured?
o: The shared server in project-scoped `.mcp.json` using environment variable expansion (e.g., `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`) so no secret is committed; the personal server in user-scoped `~/.claude.json`
Both servers in `.mcp.json`, with the token pasted in so teammates don't have to set variables
Both servers in `~/.claude.json`, with setup instructions in the wiki
The shared server in `CLAUDE.md` and the personal one in `.claude/commands/`
bank.w: Scoping follows audience: project `.mcp.json` distributes team tooling via version control, with `${VAR}` expansion keeping credentials out of the repo; `~/.claude.json` holds personal and experimental servers that stay yours. Why not the others: B commits a live secret to version control; C makes shared infrastructure a manual wiki chore that drifts; D puts server configuration in files that don't configure servers.

bank.q: A single `analyze_document` tool handles extraction, summarization, and claim verification, chosen by a mode parameter. The agent regularly picks the wrong mode and results are inconsistent. What is the recommended redesign?
o: Add a fourth mode that automatically detects the right mode
Document the modes more thoroughly inside the one description
Reduce to two modes by merging extraction into summarization
Split the generic tool into purpose-specific tools (`extract_data_points`, `summarize_content`, `verify_claim_against_source`), each with a defined input/output contract
bank.w: Purpose-specific tools turn a hidden mode decision into a visible selection decision, the thing tool descriptions are good at guiding. Each tool's contract is explicit, and misrouting drops accordingly. Why not the others: A buries the selection problem one layer deeper; B improves documentation of a structure that remains ambiguous; C reduces options while keeping the overloaded design.

bank.q: When your MCP extraction tool hits a parsing failure, it returns the message "Error: could not parse document" as an ordinary successful text result. The agent then treats that sentence as document content. What is the correct MCP pattern?
o: Prefix error text with "SYSTEM ERROR:" so the agent notices
Return the failure with the MCP `isError` flag set, so the agent programmatically recognizes a tool failure instead of interpreting error prose as data
Return an empty string on failure
Throw an unhandled exception and let the connection drop
bank.w: `isError` is MCP's channel for communicating tool failure: it makes the error a machine-recognizable condition the agent can reason about, rather than text masquerading as a successful result. Why not the others: A still relies on the model inferring failure from prose conventions; C replaces a mislabeled failure with a silent one; D turns a recoverable tool error into a transport-level breakdown.

bank.q: You have a personal `/scratch-notes` slash command you use constantly, but it reflects your own workflow and should not appear for teammates when they pull the repository. Where does the command file belong?
o: In `.claude/commands/` in the repository, like all slash commands
In the root `CLAUDE.md` under a # Commands heading
In `~/.claude/commands/` in your home directory, where user-scoped commands live outside version control
In `.claude/rules/` with a paths glob matching your username
bank.w: Command scoping mirrors intent: `~/.claude/commands/` holds personal commands visible only to you, while `.claude/commands/` in the repo is shared with everyone via version control. A personal workflow tool belongs in the former. Why not the others: A publishes a personal tool to the whole team; B is project context, not a command definition mechanism; D misuses path-scoped rules, which condition on edited file paths, not identity.

bank.q: Your `/analyze-architecture` skill produces thousands of lines of exploration output that pollute the main conversation, crowding out the task you actually wanted help with. Which `SKILL.md` frontmatter option fixes this?
o: `argument-hint`, so the skill asks what to analyze
`context: fork`, which runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context and returns results without flooding the main conversation
`allowed-tools`, restricting the skill to read-only operations
`paths`, restricting the skill to architecture files
bank.w: `context: fork` exists for exactly this: verbose or exploratory skills run in their own isolated context, and the main session receives the distilled result rather than the full exploration transcript. Why not the others: A governs parameter prompting; C governs which tools the skill may use, and neither controls where output accumulates; D is rules-file syntax, not skill frontmatter for isolation.

bank.q: You are writing a `/scaffold-component` skill that generates boilerplate files. You want a guarantee it can create files but can never run shell commands, no matter what its instructions are asked to do. How do you enforce this?
o: State "never run Bash" prominently in the `SKILL.md` instructions
Trust the skill's narrow purpose to keep it away from `Bash`
Run the skill only in plan mode
Set `allowed-tools` in the `SKILL.md` frontmatter to permit only the file-write operations the skill needs, excluding `Bash`
bank.w: `allowed-tools` is the enforcement mechanism: frontmatter-declared tool restrictions bound what the skill can invoke during execution, a configuration guarantee rather than an instruction the model might not follow. Why not the others: A is prompt-level guidance with a non-zero failure rate; B is hope; C changes the execution workflow but is not a per-skill tool restriction.

bank.q: A new teammate's Claude Code sessions ignore the team's coding standards. You discover the standards live in your own `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. What is the correct fix, and how do you verify it?
o: Move the standards into the project-level `CLAUDE.md` (checked into the repository) so every clone receives them, and use the `/memory` command to verify which memory files a session has loaded
Email the teammate your `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` to copy into their home directory
Have the teammate re-install Claude Code to refresh configuration
Paste the standards at the start of each session until they stick
bank.w: User-level configuration applies only to that user; it never travels via version control. Team standards belong at project level, and `/memory` is the diagnostic that shows exactly which memory files a session loaded. Why not the others: B distributes configuration by hand and drifts immediately; C reinstalls software to fix a file-location problem; D mistakes a persistent configuration issue for a per-session prompting task, and nothing "sticks" between sessions.

bank.q: The project's `CLAUDE.md` has grown to 2,000 lines covering testing, API conventions, deployment, and styling; sessions load it all regardless of task. What is the recommended reorganization?
o: Delete the file and rely on the model's general knowledge of good practice
Move everything to each developer's user-level `CLAUDE.md`

Split it into focused, topic-specific files in `.claude/rules/` (e.g., `testing.md`, `api-conventions.md`, `deployment.md`), adding path-scoped frontmatter where conventions apply only to matching files
Convert the entire file into a single slash command developers run manually
bank.w: The `.claude/rules/` directory is the modular alternative to a monolithic `CLAUDE.md`: focused topic files, with YAML path scoping where rules should load only for matching files, meaning less irrelevant context and easier maintenance. Why not the others: A abandons hard-won project conventions; B unshares team configuration and guarantees divergence; D makes always-relevant standards opt-in and forgettable.

bank.q: Two tasks arrive: fixing an off-by-one bug in one function with a clear stack trace, and migrating the codebase's HTTP library, touching 45+ files with several viable approaches. How should plan mode and direct execution be assigned?
o: Plan mode for both, since planning never hurts
Direct execution for both, since plan mode is only for greenfield projects
Direct execution for the well-scoped single-file bug fix; plan mode for the migration, whose scale and multiple valid approaches demand exploration and design before changes are committed
Plan mode for the bug fix and direct execution for the migration
bank.w: The assignment rule: direct execution for simple, well-scoped changes; plan mode where scale, architectural implications, or competing approaches make design-before-commitment valuable, like a 45-file migration. Why not the others: A taxes a trivial fix with ceremony; B invites costly rework by executing a large migration unplanned; D inverts the rule on both tasks.

bank.q: Developers keep invoking your `/generate-fixture` skill bare, without the entity type and record count it needs, then get confused by the results. Which frontmatter option addresses this?
o: `context: fork`, isolating the confusion in a subagent
`allowed-tools`, restricting what the skill can touch
A longer skill description explaining the parameters
`argument-hint`, which prompts developers for the required parameters when the skill is invoked without arguments
bank.w: `argument-hint` is the frontmatter mechanism for exactly this: skills that need parameters can prompt for them on bare invocation instead of running underspecified. Why not the others: A isolates output, not input requirements; B constrains tools, not arguments; C documents the parameters for whoever reads docs, but the invocation still runs bare.

bank.q: You must decide where two things live: (1) the team's universal coding standards that should shape every session, and (2) a multi-step release-notes workflow used a few times per month. What is the correct placement?
o: Both as skills, invoked when developers remember
Standards in `CLAUDE.md`, which is always loaded; the occasional release-notes workflow as a skill in `.claude/skills/`, invoked on demand
Both in `CLAUDE.md` so nothing is ever missed
Standards as a skill; the release workflow in `CLAUDE.md`
bank.w: The dividing line: `CLAUDE.md` for universal, always-relevant standards; skills for on-demand, task-specific workflows. Each mechanism carries the load it was designed for. Why not the others: A makes universal standards opt-in, so they will be skipped; C loads a monthly workflow into every session's context forever; D inverts both placements.

bank.q: Your CI job must run Claude Code non-interactively and produce review findings your pipeline can parse and post as inline PR comments. Which invocation is correct?
o: `claude "review this PR"` piped through grep to extract findings from prose
