`claude -p "review this PR"` with `--output-format json` and `--json-schema`, producing machine-parseable structured findings without waiting for interactive input
`claude --batch "review this PR" --format=structured`
`claude -p "review this PR"` alone, then regex-parsing the prose output
bank.w: The CI trio: `-p` (`--print`) for non-interactive execution, `--output-format json` for machine-readable output, and `--json-schema` to enforce the findings structure your pipeline consumes: no prose parsing, no input hangs. Why not the others: A hangs waiting for interactive input and then scrapes prose; C invents flags that do not exist; D solves the hang but leaves the pipeline regex-parsing unstructured text.

bank.q: CI-generated tests ignore your team's fixture library, duplicate helper setup, and test trivialities. Developers reject most of them. What is the configuration-level fix?
o: Generate three times as many tests so some survive review
Have developers rewrite the generated tests as a standing chore
Lower the temperature of the generation call
Document testing standards, what makes a test valuable, and the available fixtures in `CLAUDE.md`, the mechanism that supplies project context to CI-invoked Claude Code
bank.w: CI invocations get their project context from `CLAUDE.md`. Standards, value criteria, and fixture documentation there directly raise generation quality: the model can only follow conventions it has been shown. Why not the others: A scales the reject pile; B institutionalizes rework instead of fixing its cause; C reduces variability of output that is uninformed either way.

bank.q: Reviews re-run after each new commit to a PR, and the bot re-posts the same findings every time; developers now mute it. How should re-reviews be designed?
o: Include the prior review's findings in context and instruct Claude to report only new issues or previously reported ones that remain unaddressed
Review only the newest commit's diff in isolation
Limit reviews to one per PR regardless of subsequent commits
Post all findings again but formatted differently to seem new
bank.w: Duplicate suppression is a context design problem: give the reviewer its own prior findings and the explicit instruction to report deltas (new issues plus unresolved carryovers), and the noise stops while coverage remains complete. Why not the others: B misses issues that emerge from interaction with earlier commits; C leaves everything after the first push unreviewed; D disguises the spam developers already muted.

bank.q: You notice that when the same Claude Code session that generated a change also reviews it, the review is conspicuously gentle, missing issues an independent reviewer catches. Why, and what is the design implication?
o: The model is being polite; instruct it to be harsher
Reviews should always be performed by a larger model tier
A session retains the reasoning context from generation, making it less likely to question its own decisions, so CI reviews should run in an independent instance without the generator's context
Generation and review must run on different days to avoid contamination
bank.w: Session context isolation matters for review integrity: the generating session carries the rationale that produced the code, biasing it toward its own choices. An independent instance evaluates the code on its own terms. Why not the others: A misreads a context effect as a personality setting; B changes capability when the problem is contaminated context (the same model reviews well when independent); D adds superstition to a mechanism that is about context, not calendars.

bank.q: Your review prompt says "be conservative and only report high-confidence findings," yet false positives remain high. What does effective precision engineering look like instead?
o: Add "be very, very conservative" for stronger emphasis
Report all findings but sort them by the model's stated confidence
Reduce the number of files reviewed per run
Replace confidence language with explicit categorical criteria: define which issue types to report (bugs, security) and which to skip (minor style, local patterns), with concrete boundaries
bank.w: Vague conservatism doesn't transfer; specific criteria do. Defining reportable versus skippable categories with concrete boundaries gives the model an operable decision rule, which is what actually moves precision. Why not the others: A intensifies an instruction that has no operational content; B reorders noise instead of reducing it, and self-stated confidence is poorly calibrated; C reviews less code with the same faulty judgment.

bank.q: Findings in the "code style" category are 70% false positives, and developers have begun dismissing security findings too; trust in the whole reviewer is collapsing. What is the right operational move?
o: Ship more style findings to demonstrate the category's importance
Temporarily disable the style category to restore trust in the accurate categories, while improving the style prompts before re-enabling it
Rename "code style" to "code quality"
Ask developers to be more tolerant of noise during the tuning period
bank.w: High false-positive categories are contagious: they teach developers to dismiss everything. Disabling the offender protects the credibility of accurate categories while its prompts are fixed offline; trust is the system's real asset. Why not the others: A doubles down on the noise destroying trust; C relabels the same false positives; D asks humans to absorb a cost the configuration should eliminate.

bank.q: The reviewer labels near-identical issues "critical" one day and "minor" the next. Severity-based merge gates are therefore unreliable. How do you get consistent severity classification?
o: Define explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each level, so every severity has an operational definition the model can match against
Remove severity levels and treat all findings equally
Let the model choose severity freely but average it over five runs
Map severity to line count of the affected code
bank.w: Consistency comes from operational definitions: severity levels anchored by concrete examples give the classifier something to match, turning a vibe into a rubric. That is what makes severity gates dependable. Why not the others: B discards the signal the merge gate needs; C statistically launders an unanchored judgment; D measures size, not impact: a one-line auth bypass outranks a fifty-line comment tweak.

bank.q: The reviewer keeps flagging your codebase's accepted idiomatic patterns (e.g., intentional fall-throughs with comments) as bugs, while your detailed prose instructions haven't fixed it. What is the most effective addition?
o: A rule that anything containing a comment is acceptable
An instruction to "use good judgment about idioms"
Few-shot examples distinguishing the accepted patterns from genuine issues, showing the reasoning why each is or isn't reportable, so the model generalizes the judgment to novel cases
A ban on reviewing files containing any idiomatic pattern
bank.w: When prose fails to convey a judgment boundary, examples carry it: contrasted acceptable-versus-genuine cases with reasoning teach a distinction the model can generalize, the documented strength of few-shot prompting for false-positive reduction. Why not the others: A creates a trivially wrong rule any commented bug defeats; B restates the goal without transferring the judgment; D exempts exactly the code that most needs reviewing.

bank.q: Your team is deciding which CI workloads to move to the Message Batches API for its 50% cost savings. Which statement is accurate?
o: Batches are guaranteed to complete within one hour
The batch API supports multi-turn tool calling within a single request
Blocking workflows such as pre-merge checks should stay on the synchronous API, since batches can take up to 24 hours with no latency SLA
Batch responses cannot be matched back to their requests
bank.w: Anything a developer waits on cannot tolerate a 24-hour, no-SLA window and stays synchronous. The other side of the same rule: latency-tolerant, non-blocking workloads like nightly test generation and weekly audit reports are the ideal profile for the batch discount. Why not the others: A and B are false (there is no latency guarantee, and mid-request tool execution is unsupported); D is false, since `custom_id` exists precisely to correlate request/response pairs.

bank.q: You are adding few-shot examples to the review prompt. Which practice reflects how few-shot prompting works best?
o: Include as many examples as possible (twenty or more) to cover every case
Use 2–4 targeted examples aimed at the ambiguous scenarios, showing the reasoning for why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives
Once examples are added, explicit criteria become unnecessary
Rely on examples only for prose tasks; they don't work for code
bank.w: Effective few-shot work is targeted: a handful of examples aimed at genuine ambiguity, with reasoning shown; quality of targeting over quantity. A complementary practice is including examples that demonstrate the exact desired output format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix) to achieve consistent, actionable findings. Why not the others: A bloats context and dilutes the signal of the examples that matter; C and D are false: examples complement explicit criteria, and code review is a prime few-shot use case.

bank.q: Your current pipeline asks Claude to "respond with JSON" in plain text; downstream parsing breaks on markdown fences, trailing commentary, and occasional malformed syntax. What is the most reliable structural fix?
o: Strengthen the prompt: "respond ONLY with valid JSON, no exceptions"
Post-process the text with regexes that strip fences and repair syntax
Define the extraction as a tool whose input schema is your JSON schema, and read the structured data from the `tool_use` block, guaranteeing schema-compliant output and eliminating JSON syntax errors
Switch to XML output, which models format more carefully
bank.w: Tool use with JSON schemas is the reliability mechanism for structured output: the model's extraction arrives as schema-conformant tool input, not as prose that happens to contain JSON, so syntax errors are eliminated by construction. Why not the others: A improves the odds within a fundamentally text-shaped channel; B patches symptoms with fragile repairs; D relocates the same free-text problem to a different syntax.

bank.q: You have several extraction tools, one per document type, and incoming documents of unknown type. The model must always produce a structured extraction, choosing the appropriate schema itself, and never reply with conversational text. Which `tool_choice` setting is correct?
o: `tool_choice`: "any", so the model must call a tool but may choose which, guaranteeing structured output while leaving schema selection to the model
`tool_choice`: "auto", so the model decides whether to call a tool at all
`tool_choice` forced to one named tool, applied to every document
Omit `tool_choice`, since defaults handle this
bank.w: The three modes map to intent: "any" compels a tool call while preserving the model's choice among schemas, exactly right for unknown document types that must always yield structured output. Why not the others: B (and D, which defaults to it) permits conversational text instead of a tool call; C welds every document to one schema when types vary.

bank.q: Your invoice schema marks `vendor_tax_id` as required. On invoices that genuinely lack a tax ID, the model fabricates plausible-looking values to satisfy the schema. What is the schema-level fix?
o: Add a prompt instruction: "never fabricate tax IDs"
Post-validate tax IDs against a checksum and discard failures
Lower the temperature to make fabrication less creative
Make the field optional/nullable so the model can legitimately return null when the information is absent from the source document
bank.w: Required fields on possibly-absent information force fabrication: the schema leaves no honest answer. Nullable/optional fields give the model a legitimate way to say "not present," which is the designed prevention for this failure. Why not the others: A pits an instruction against a structural requirement that demands a value; B catches well-formed fabrications only by luck; C makes invented values more conservative-looking, not less invented.

bank.q: Since adopting tool use, extractions are always syntactically valid, yet invoices arrive where line items don't sum to the stated total, and values occasionally land in the wrong fields. What should you understand and do?
o: Schema compliance was falsely advertised; file a bug

Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors but not semantic ones; add semantic validation, e.g., extracting `calculated_total` alongside `stated_total` and flagging discrepancies with a `conflict_detected` boolean
Make every field an unconstrained string so nothing can be wrong
Re-run each extraction until the numbers happen to sum
bank.w: The boundary of the guarantee: tool use ensures structure, not truth. Semantic errors (sums that don't reconcile, transposed fields) need a semantic validation layer, with self-check fields like `calculated_total` making discrepancies machine-visible. Why not the others: A misunderstands what was promised: shape, not semantics; C destroys the structure that downstream systems depend on; D retries until errors align by chance rather than detecting them.

bank.q: An extraction fails Pydantic validation with two specific field errors. You will retry. What should the retry request contain, and when would you skip retrying altogether?
o: Just the instruction "try again more carefully"; skip retries on Mondays
Only the validation errors, to keep the retry cheap; always retry at least five times

The original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors, enabling targeted self-correction; skip retrying when the required information is simply absent from the source, since no retry can produce it
A different document, to give the model a fresh start
bank.w: Retry-with-error-feedback works because the model sees what it produced, what was wrong, and the source to correct against. And the boundary matters: format and structural errors are retryable; information absent from the document is not. Why not the others: A retries blind, since the model can't fix errors it isn't shown; B removes the document and extraction the correction must reference; D abandons the failed extraction rather than repairing it.

bank.q: An overnight batch of 10,000 documents completes with 200 failures: most are oversized documents that blew past context limits, plus some transient errors. What is the correct failure-handling workflow?
o: Identify the failed requests by `custom_id` and resubmit only those, with modifications where needed, e.g., chunking the oversized documents before resubmission
Resubmit the entire 10,000-document batch and keep whichever results arrive first
Discard the 200 failures as an acceptable loss rate
Switch the 200 failures to the synchronous API unchanged, where context limits don't apply
bank.w: `custom_id` exists for exactly this: correlate failures to their source documents, fix what caused each failure (chunk the oversized ones), and resubmit only the fixed subset, paying again for 200 documents, not 10,000. Why not the others: B reprocesses 9,800 successes to retry 200 failures; C silently drops 2% of the corpus; D misunderstands context limits, which belong to the model, not the API path: unchunked oversized documents fail synchronously too.

bank.q: A customer's first message is: "I want to speak to a human. Do not try to fix this yourself." The issue looks like a routine replacement the agent could resolve. What should the agent do?
o: Attempt resolution first, escalating only if the attempt fails
Run sentiment analysis and escalate only if frustration exceeds a threshold
Escalate immediately: an explicit customer request for a human is honored without first attempting investigation
Ask the customer three clarifying questions before deciding
bank.w: Explicit customer demands for a human are a first-class escalation trigger, honored immediately. Overriding a stated preference to demonstrate capability damages trust regardless of how resolvable the issue looks. Why not the others: A and D do exactly what the customer forbade; B substitutes an unreliable proxy (sentiment) for a signal that could not be clearer: the customer already said the words.

bank.q: In long multi-issue sessions, the agent's later responses misquote refund amounts and order numbers because earlier details were condensed into vague summaries, while each `lookup_order` result dumps 40+ fields into context. Which change prevents the misquoted amounts and order numbers?
o: Extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses) into a persistent case-facts block included in each prompt, outside the summarized history
Increase `max_tokens` so responses can be longer
Summarize even more aggressively to save space
Ask the customer to repeat key numbers periodically
bank.w: Protect precise transactional facts from lossy summarization by persisting them in a dedicated block outside the summarized history. A complementary practice is stopping the bloat at its source by trimming each tool result to the fields relevant to the current issue before it enters context. Why not the others: B controls output length, not context quality; C intensifies the exact failure mode, numbers dissolving into vagueness; D outsources the system's memory problem to the customer.

bank.q: Mid-way through an extended exploration session, context is filling with verbose discovery output and responses are noticeably degrading, but you are not ready to end the session. Which built-in command helps immediately?
o: `/memory`, which clears the conversation
`/fork`, which splits the session in half
`/compact`, which reduces context usage by compacting the conversation so the session can continue productively
`/rules`, which reloads the rule files
bank.w: `/compact` is the in-session relief valve for exactly this situation: it compacts accumulated context, typically bloated with verbose discovery output, so an extended session can continue without degradation. Why not the others: A shows which memory files are loaded (diagnostic, not cleanup); B is not the mechanism (forking is for divergent branches, not compression); D does not address conversation bloat.

bank.q: During multi-hour codebase exploration sessions, the agent starts answering from "typical patterns" instead of the specific classes it discovered earlier. Which practice counteracts this context degradation?
o: Switch to a model with a larger context window and continue accumulating
Maintain a scratchpad file recording key findings as they are discovered, and have the agent reference it for subsequent questions
Repeat important questions twice in the same message
Ask the agent to be more specific
bank.w: A scratchpad persists precise findings outside the degrading conversation, so later answers rest on what was actually discovered. A complementary practice is delegating verbose investigation (e.g., "find all test files", "trace the refund flow") to subagents that return summaries, keeping the main session's context for high-level coordination. Why not the others: A postpones the same degradation at higher cost; C and D add more text to an already saturated context without removing any of the noise causing the problem.

bank.q: Final reports state findings but cite nothing. Investigation shows each summarization step compresses source attribution away, so by synthesis time nobody knows which claim came from where. What is the structural fix?
o: Have the report generator add plausible citations at the end
Instruct the synthesis agent to write "sources available on request"
Require subagents to output structured claim-source mappings (claim, evidence excerpt, source URL or document name) that every downstream agent preserves and merges through synthesis
Reduce the number of summarization steps to one
bank.w: Provenance survives only if it is structural: claim-source mappings travel as data through every hop, so synthesis merges attributed claims instead of anonymous assertions. Attribution is preserved, never reconstructed. Why not the others: A invents citations, worse than none in a research product; B advertises attribution the system no longer possesses; D reduces compression events but the remaining one still strips attribution.

bank.q: Two credible sources report different figures for the same market's size, and one subagent's summary simply picked the larger number. Which practice produces correct handling of conflicting source data?
o: Annotate the conflict explicitly (both values, each with source attribution) and let the coordinator decide how to reconcile before synthesis, rather than silently selecting one
Average the two figures into a single compromise value
Always adopt the more recent source and discard the other
Exclude both sources to avoid taking sides
bank.w: Conflicts are information: preserve both values with attribution and surface the disagreement for deliberate reconciliation. A complementary practice is requiring publication or data-collection dates in subagents' structured outputs, since "conflicting" figures often just measure different moments. Why not the others: B invents a number no source reported; C automates a reconciliation that needs judgment (recency is context, not an override rule); D deletes two credible sources because they disagree.

bank.q: You are designing how the web search subagent behaves when its searches fail or return nothing. Which behavior is correct?
o: On any failure, immediately terminate the entire research workflow
Return empty results marked as success whenever a search fails, keeping the pipeline moving
Report every problem as a generic "search unavailable" status
Distinguish access failures (timeouts, service errors) from valid empty results (successful queries with no matches), since the two require different coordinator decisions
bank.w: Resilient error propagation is honest: never conflate "the search broke" with "the search found nothing", because the coordinator decides differently in each case. A complementary practice is attempting local recovery for transient failures (e.g., retrying a timeout) and propagating to the coordinator only errors it cannot resolve, including what was attempted and any partial results. Why not the others: A makes any single failure fatal when partial-result strategies exist; B is silent suppression, failure dressed as fact; C hides the very context that recovery decisions need.

bank.q: Your extraction system reports 97% aggregate accuracy, and leadership wants to cut human review of high-confidence extractions. Which practice must precede that decision?
o: Segment accuracy by document type and field, verifying consistent performance across all segments, since aggregate metrics can mask systematic failures on specific types
Accept the 97% aggregate as sufficient evidence on its own
Stop measuring once review is reduced, to save cost
Review only extractions the model itself flags as uncertain
bank.w: Segmentation proves the average isn't hiding a failing document type or field. A complementary safeguard is stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions, which keeps measuring the error rate after the humans step back and catches drift and novel error patterns. Why not the others: B trusts exactly the number that masks segment failures; C removes the instrumentation precisely when risk increases; D trusts self-flagged uncertainty, which misses the errors the model is confidently wrong about.

bank.q: Reviewer capacity covers only a fraction of extractions, so review attention must be routed where errors are likeliest. Which practice is the foundation of a sound routing design?
o: Trust the model's raw self-reported confidence scores without validation
Have the model output field-level confidence scores, then calibrate review thresholds against a labeled validation set
Review a fixed 1% of extractions chosen by submission order
Review only documents longer than ten pages
bank.w: Field-level confidence scores become meaningful once thresholds are tuned on labeled data; calibration is what makes them a usable routing signal. The routing step that follows: send to human review the extractions with low calibrated confidence or ambiguous/contradictory source documents, where errors concentrate. Why not the others: A uses uncalibrated confidence, the known-unreliable version of the right signal; C and D route by arrival order and page count, neither of which correlates with error risk.
